Key: ENG-19977

Title: Service Sentry: per-tenant/model adaptive trip thresholds and deterministic safe fallbacks

Status: In Progress

Assignee: Liam O'Neill

## Labels

- slo
  - failover
  - circuit-safety
  - tenant-isolation
  - observability
  - load-shedding

## Dependencies

- ENG-16234
  - ENG-27481

Release: runtime-2.1

Security Review Required: false

Description: Goal: Implement a runtime 'Service Sentry' layer that maintains adaptive per-entity (tenant/model/dependency) trip thresholds and provides deterministic and safe fallback behaviors for host-level and regional failures. This ticket covers algorithm design, runtime integration, rollout plan, and observability requirements. The intent is to reduce customer-visible errors during transient overloads or degraded downstreams while maintaining SLOs and predictable cost behavior.

Background And Rationale: Current circuit breaker approaches are global or per-service with static thresholds which either trip too aggressively for low-volume tenants or too slowly for noisy tenants. We need an adaptive, composable mechanism that accounts for entity volume, multi-region health, and model-tail latency distributions. It should be deterministic (so rollbacks and debugging are straightforward) and produce a safe fallback when a primary model or region is unhealthy.

Micro-experiments (design notes)
1) Latency-tail canary (14 days)
- Goal: validate P99 sensitivity to batching and cache warmup.
- Method: route 5% traffic to a variant with mid-size batch window + KV cache priming; collect P95/P99 delta and token cost delta.
- Success criteria: P99 reduced by >= 15% without >5% increase in token cost.
- Safety: auto-fail on 1.5x error rate.

2) Error-budget burn simulation (chaos-lite)
- Goal: ensure runbooks map to real-world mitigation steps and that escalations run end-to-end.
- Method: synthetic traffic spike + injected transient 502 on one downstream for 30m. Observe detection, pager time-to-ack, and mitigation path.
- Success criteria: detection <5m, mitigation action taken <15m, customer-visible error <1% of normal load.

- Metrics: standardized names and units (latency_ms.p95, latency_ms.p99, errors.5xx.rate, cache.hit_rate).
- Dashboards: one-liner summary + drilldowns for tail latency, queued requests, dependency graph.
- Alerts: threshold-based + anomaly detector for residuals; alert includes runbook link and suggested mitigations.

- One-line symptom-to-action map.
- Quick triage checklist (3 steps).
- Top 3 mitigation levers (e.g., reduce batch, increase pool, enable fallback model).
- Rollback steps and known side-effects.

Signals, tentative metrics and starter targets (provisional — iterate after telemetry baseline):

Focus: translate product-level availability and correctness expectations into measurable signals, ownership, integration tasks, and a pragmatic rollout path that minimizes customer impact while improving long-term observability and remediation speed.
- Audience: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, Observability, Product-Hosted-API, Solutions Eng, Support.

High-level objectives (what success looks like):
1) Observable, actionable signals for the top three failure modes across model-serving (model-load failures, KV cache regressions, tail-latency spikes).
2) Clear ownership and runbooks for each signal with measurable reduction targets in MTTD/MTTR over rolling 90-day windows.
3) A staged SLO adoption pattern that lets teams opt into strict error/latency targets with canary rollouts and automated fallback policies.
4) Two pilot services on dedicated infra with full pipeline (dashboards, alerts, automated rollback) within Q3 2026.

Guiding principles:
- Incremental: instrument first, then set targets, then automate responses.
- Customer-impact focused: prioritize signals that map to user-visible degradation.
- Low blast radius: use progressive rollout (canary, cohort) for any enforcement.
- Cross-team pairing: each milestone requires an SRE + owning-engineer co-shipper.

Scope (in):
- Model-serving control plane and inference runtime path (request ingress, KV cache, model weights load, token generation latency).
- Observability (metrics, traces, logs) and alerting pipelines used by SRE and product teams.
- Runbooks and automated remediation playbooks.

- Deep model quality evaluation (LLM hallucination metrics) — covered by Optimize/product.

# Service Sentry: per-tenant/model adaptive trip thresholds and deterministic safe fallbacks

Key: ENG-19977

Team: engineering

Title: Service Sentry: per-tenant/model adaptive trip thresholds and deterministic safe fallbacks

Status: In Progress

Priority: P1

Created At: 2026-02-18

Updated At: 2026-03-12

Creator: Samira Cho

Assignee: Liam O'Neill

Project: Reliability: Multi-region Resilience

Cycle: 2026-W10

Estimate: 5

Due Date: 2026-03-31

## Labels

- slo
  - failover
  - circuit-safety
  - tenant-isolation
  - observability
  - load-shedding

## Dependencies

- ENG-16234
  - ENG-27481

Release: runtime-2.1

Security Review Required: false

Description: Goal: Implement a runtime 'Service Sentry' layer that maintains adaptive per-entity (tenant/model/dependency) trip thresholds and provides deterministic and safe fallback behaviors for host-level and regional failures. This ticket covers algorithm design, runtime integration, rollout plan, and observability requirements. The intent is to reduce customer-visible errors during transient overloads or degraded downstreams while maintaining SLOs and predictable cost behavior.

Background And Rationale: Current circuit breaker approaches are global or per-service with static thresholds which either trip too aggressively for low-volume tenants or too slowly for noisy tenants. We need an adaptive, composable mechanism that accounts for entity volume, multi-region health, and model-tail latency distributions. It should be deterministic (so rollbacks and debugging are straightforward) and produce a safe fallback when a primary model or region is unhealthy.

## Acceptance Criteria

Micro-experiments (design notes)
1) Latency-tail canary (14 days)
- Goal: validate P99 sensitivity to batching and cache warmup.
- Method: route 5% traffic to a variant with mid-size batch window + KV cache priming; collect P95/P99 delta and token cost delta.
- Success criteria: P99 reduced by >= 15% without >5% increase in token cost.
- Safety: auto-fail on 1.5x error rate.

2) Error-budget burn simulation (chaos-lite)
- Goal: ensure runbooks map to real-world mitigation steps and that escalations run end-to-end.
- Method: synthetic traffic spike + injected transient 502 on one downstream for 30m. Observe detection, pager time-to-ack, and mitigation path.
- Success criteria: detection <5m, mitigation action taken <15m, customer-visible error <1% of normal load.

Observability contracts (minimal)
- Metrics: standardized names and units (latency_ms.p95, latency_ms.p99, errors.5xx.rate, cache.hit_rate).
- Dashboards: one-liner summary + drilldowns for tail latency, queued requests, dependency graph.
- Alerts: threshold-based + anomaly detector for residuals; alert includes runbook link and suggested mitigations.

Runbook composition checklist (for each service)
- One-line symptom-to-action map.
- Quick triage checklist (3 steps).
- Top 3 mitigation levers (e.g., reduce batch, increase pool, enable fallback model).
- Rollback steps and known side-effects.
- Postmortem owner & SLAs for documentation.

- Two-tiered remediation: soft (automated routing adjustments + throttling) and hard (circuit-breaker open -> degrade to fallback model or region failover).

Measurement details (examples):
- Availability SLI: fraction of requests returning 2xx with valid model output within deadline. Measure window: 30d rolling and 5m for burn-rate detection.
- Latency SLI: p95/p99 of server processing time (start of handler to final token produced). Target example: p95 < 300ms, p99 < 1200ms for low-latency tier.
- Model-quality SLI: % of a sampled production prompt-set that passes acceptance checks (semantic match / hallucination threshold). Evaluate hourly on a reservoir-sampled set of 1k prompts per model.
- Cardinality: compute SLIs per (route, model_variant, region, customer_tier). Aggregations apply weighted averaging where weight = request count / tokens to reflect economic impact.

Error budget math (example):
- Goal: 99.9% availability over 30d. Budget = 0.1% of requests. If baseline is 10M requests/day, monthly budget ~30M * 0.001 = 30k requests.
- Burn rate calculation window: 1h and 6h short-term windows to detect incidents. Burn rate = observed failures / expected allowed failures in window. If burn_rate > 2 for 1h -> soft remediation; burn_rate > 8 for 1h -> hard remediation. Values adjustable per tier.

Circuit breaker design notes:
- CB is scoped at three levels: route, model-variant, and customer. Each level maintains independent state with hierarchical precedence (customer > route > model).
- States: CLOSED, RECOVERING (half-open probe traffic), OPEN.
- Metrics to trigger OPEN: consecutive failure ratio above threshold (e.g., 10% failure over 1m and burn_rate > 4), p

This document is a curated catalog of realistic runtime rollback scenarios for the Redwood serving platform, paired with a deterministic SLO impact mapping and step-by-step operator checklists. ----------------
- Rollbacks are common and high-risk; ad-hoc decisions increase blast radius.

Content: Summary:
This document defines the stakeholder status matrix, callout and escalation protocol, on-call succession rules, and standardized status-page and customer communication templates for all multi-service incidents affecting Redwood Inference. It consolidates the lifecycle from first detection -> bridge -> customer notice -> postmortem archival, and prescribes time-boxed SLAs for each phase.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Reduce confusion in cross-functional incidents by clarifying who is notified, when, and how, and providing pre-approved message templates for public (customer-facing) and private (internal/legal) channels.
- Scope: Applies to all incidents with potential customer impact for Redwood-hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Excludes internal-only tooling outages without customer visibility (see "service impact tiers").

Key contacts and ownership:
- Incident Commander (IC): service owner for the impacted product line (primary responsibility: mitigation decisions, major comms)
- Bridge Operator: SRE on rotation (runs bridge, maintains timeline, posts updates)
- Customer Liaison: Customer Success rep or Solutions Engineer assigned for affected customers
- Legal & Security: Called in for incidents with data exposure or regulatory implications
- External Communications: Marketing/PR for elevated public statements

Service impact tiers (decision table):
1) Tier 0 — Informational
   - Symptom: Internal metric drift, non-customer-facing alert.
   - Action: Annotate dashboard, triage in regular backlog. No on-call invocation.
2) Tier 1 — Degraded but functional
   - Symptom: Increased latency, partial error rate affecting <5% customer traffic, SLA degradation risk.
   - Action: On-call alert -> Bridge if sustained >15 minutes. Customer status page update: optional.
3) Tier 2 — Partial outage
   - Symptom: Significant errors or latency affecting >=5% but <50% customers, feature-limited behavior.
   - Action: Immediate bridge, customer notification within 30 minutes, regular updates every 30 minutes.
4) Tier 3 — Major outage / data integrity risk

This guidance is intentionally conservative: a “works on paper” failover that has not been drilled can increase customer impact during real incidents.

## Scope and non-goals
### In scope
- Private deployments running Redwood’s serving and/or control-plane components in customer-managed environments.
- Multi-region routing patterns (DNS, L7 proxy, anycast/edge steering) and operational playbooks.
- Recommended health signal sources, dampening, and rollback/anti-flap guardrails.

### Out of scope
- A bespoke, fully managed, per-customer automated failover controller equivalent to Hosted/Dedicated.
- Multi-cloud migrations or re-architecting customer applications.

## Definitions
- **Region-level impairment:** A sustained inability to serve requests from a region due to dependency loss (network reachability, control plane, storage, capacity) rather than a single component regression.
- **Failover:** Shifting traffic from Region A to Region B (or rebalancing across regions) based on a pre-defined policy and triggers.
- **Failback:** Returning traffic to the original region after recovery. Failback must be treated as a change event with explicit safety checks.
- **Blast radius:** The maximum scope of traffic/tenants/routes that can be affected by an automated or operator-initiated failover.

## Support model: customer-managed vs Redwood-assisted
Redwood Private deployments vary significantly (networking, IAM/KMS, adjacent platform components). To avoid ambiguity during incidents, align on the support model **before** enabling multi-region.

### Model A — Customer-managed failover (recommended default)
**Customer owns**:
- Traffic steering (DNS, load balancer, API gateway, service mesh).
- Health checks and failover triggers.
- Regional capacity planning and admission control.
- Replication strategy for any stateful dependencies.",

### Pattern 4 — L7 proxy / global gateway steering (best control; more moving parts)
**Description:** A customer-operated global gateway routes to regional backends based on health and policy.

**Pros**
- Fast detection and steering.
- Fine-grained routing (per-tenant/per-route/per-model).

**Cons**
- Gateway becomes a critical dependency; must be multi-region itself.

**Guidance**
- Ensure the gateway’s own failover does not create a single point of failure.
- Explicitly tune timeouts/retries to avoid amplifying regional impairments.

## Prerequisites checklist (must-have)
The following prerequisites should be met before enabling any automatic or semi-automatic regional failover.

### 1) Region parity and capacity
- **Model availability:** Target models (and exact versions) are present in all participating regions.
- **Capacity headroom:** Each region can absorb the expected failover load.
  - For Active/Standby: validate the standby region can serve **100%** of critical traffic (or define a documented degradation plan).
  - For Active/Active: validate each region can absorb an additional **+50–80%** burst depending on your steady-state split.
- **Autoscaling behavior:** Ensure scaling does not depend on impaired regional services (e.g., metrics pipeline in the same region).

### 2) Data residency and compliance constraints
- Define allowed failover destinations per tenant/workload.
- Confirm whether prompts, outputs, logs, and traces may cross borders.
- Ensure audit logging meets your requirements for “who changed steering and why.”

See: **Failover and Security Boundaries** (related page).

### 3) Networking and reachability
- Cross-region connectivity is validated for:
  - Client → gateway/entrypoint
  - Gateway → regional serving endpoints
  - Control plane dependencies (if centralized)
  - Any private peering (VPN/Interconnect) paths
- Synthetic probes exist and are monitored from at least two independent vantage points.",

two primary regions (us-east-1 and us-west-2) with cross-region health checks and smart routing. Traffic is routed by policy at the edge; when a region shows degraded health we shift new sessions automatically to the healthy region. Persistent telemetry and audit logs are replicated to an object store with cross-region replication.

2) RTO / RPO by workload (targets):
- Synchronous low-latency text generation endpoints: RTO target = 3 minutes for request routing & DNS/edge reroute; functional RTO to reach comparable latency P90 = 8-12 minutes (primarily warm-up for model caches). RPO target = near-zero for request logs and audit events (replicated within 30s), RPO = best-effort for in-flight partial responses (we mark these as lost and surface retry logic).
- Streaming/chat sessions with KV cache: RTO target = 5 minutes to re-establish routing; functional RTO to restore full cache-hit parity = 10-20 minutes depending on active session size. RPO = minutes for KV cache state (we continuously write checkpoints to replicated storage; last checkpoint typically within 60s).
- Batch/async embeddings ingestion: RTO target = 15 minutes; RPO = near-zero for persisted ingestion queues (replicated across regions).

3) Multi-region failover behavior and steps (automatic):
- Monitoring: edge probes, regional health monitors, and model-serving heartbeat metrics.
- Triggering: automatic routing switch when regional health falls below thresholds (configurable per-customer).
- Failover actions: 1) edge DNS and routing updates; 2) model serving processes in healthy region accept new traffic; 3) prefix/KV cache warm-up begins using prioritized checkpoint replay; 4) telemetry continues to replicate to central store.
- Fallback policy: we maintain a warm standby of model weights on GPUs in the secondary region (quantized formats), enabling faster warm-up for commonly used models. Customers can choose more aggressive warm standby (higher cost) for sub-1-minute recovery.

   - Policy is hybrid: threshold-based trip + ML-ish scoring that weights correlated signals. Breaker states: CLOSED, SOFT-OPEN (reject background and long-running ops), OPEN (reject non-critical control-plane changes), ISOLATED (network/compute gated until manual or automated recovery).
   - Hysteresis: exponential backoff with jitter and a minimum cool-down of 3 minutes, plus accelerated recovery if downstream metrics normalize.

3) Multi-region failover choreography:
   - Use progressive siphoning: initiate partial diversion to target region for low-risk traffic, measure real-time health and ramp if success. If target region metrics degrade >stop thresholds, abort and fallback to a safety region or degrade workloads.
   - Maintain per-region capacity manifests; routing service consults available capacity and tenant prioritization (critical customers get higher queue weight).
   - Rationale: full instant cutover is too brittle; progressive approach reduces wide-scale cascading.

constraints (capacity, data residency, network reachability, and control plane dependencies).
- Day-2 operational caveats (testing, observability, change management, and incident coordination).

This guidance is intentionally conservative: a “works on paper” failover that has not been drilled can increase customer impact during real incidents.

## Scope and non-goals
### In scope
- Private deployments running Redwood’s serving and/or control-plane components in customer-managed environments.
- Multi-region routing patterns (DNS, L7 proxy, anycast/edge steering) and operational playbooks.
- Recommended health signal sources, dampening, and rollback/anti-flap guardrails.

### Out of scope
- A bespoke, fully managed, per-customer automated failover controller equivalent to Hosted/Dedicated.
- Multi-cloud migrations or re-architecting customer applications.

## Definitions
- **Region-level impairment:** A sustained inability to serve requests from a region due to dependency loss (network reachability, control plane, storage, capacity) rather than a single component regression.
- **Failover:** Shifting traffic from Region A to Region B (or rebalancing across regions) based on a pre-defined policy and triggers.
- **Failback:** Returning traffic to the original region after recovery. Failback must be treated as a change event with explicit safety checks.
- **Blast radius:** The maximum scope of traffic/tenants/routes that can be affected by an automated or operator-initiated failover.

## Support model: customer-managed vs Redwood-assisted
Redwood Private deployments vary significantly (networking, IAM/KMS, adjacent platform components). To avoid ambiguity during incidents, align on the support model **before** enabling multi-region.

### Model A — Customer-managed failover (recommended default)
**Customer owns**:
- Traffic steering (DNS, load balancer, API gateway, service mesh).
- Health checks and failover triggers.
- Regional capacity planning and admission control.
- Replication strategy for any stateful dependencies.

- Phase 0 - Detection: Confirm cross-region scope using global latency dashboard, p95/p99 error heatmap, and dedicated pool telemetry (GPU OOMs, scheduling failures). Use tag 'cross-region' in the incident room.
  - Phase 1 - Containment: If two or more regions show sustained p95 > 2x baseline AND error rate increase > 3x, initiate cross-region failover protocol.
  - Phase 2 - Traffic Shift Preparation: Verify capacity in candidate target region (available GPU slots, model variant compatibility, matching quantization profiles). Check KV cache hit rate history and plan for warmup time (estimate warmup RTT per prefix).
  - Phase 3 - Traffic Shift Execution (manual steps):
  -   1) Enter maintenance window in Console for affected routes and pause background billing-heavy tasks for dedicated customers as needed.
  -   2) Adjust Smart Routing weights: set primary region weight to 0.1 and target region to 0.9 in increments (0 -> 10% -> 50% -> 90%) with 2 minute observation between steps.
  -   3) If using DNS-based mitigation, ensure global LB TTL <= 60s before initiating. Prefer global LB weight updates over DNS for lower lead time.
  -   4) Warm KV caches via /internal/cache-warm for top 200 prefixes and run a controlled synthetic load at 5-10% of production RPS to pre-fill caches.
  -   5) Validate functional correctness: run smoke tests (generation, chat, embeddings) against target region and compare outputs against golden prompts (allowing model-variant deltas).
  - Phase 4 - Post-shift Validation: Monitor p50/p95/p99 latency, error rates, and client-side observed timeouts for 30 minutes at steady traffic. Ensure SLOs return to acceptable thresholds. If regression observed, revert weights by 50% or fall back to canary route.
  - Phase 5 - Rollback Criteria: Define automatic rollback triggers: sustained >15% error rate increase, p99 > 3x baseline

- Avoid frequent flips; use hold-down timers (see Triggering & guardrails).

### Pattern 4 — L7 proxy / global gateway steering (best control; more moving parts)
**Description:** A customer-operated global gateway routes to regional backends based on health and policy.

**Pros**
- Fast detection and steering.
- Fine-grained routing (per-tenant/per-route/per-model).

**Cons**
- Gateway becomes a critical dependency; must be multi-region itself.

**Guidance**
- Ensure the gateway’s own failover does not create a single point of failure.
- Explicitly tune timeouts/retries to avoid amplifying regional impairments.

## Prerequisites checklist (must-have)
The following prerequisites should be met before enabling any automatic or semi-automatic regional failover.

### 1) Region parity and capacity
- **Model availability:** Target models (and exact versions) are present in all participating regions.
- **Capacity headroom:** Each region can absorb the expected failover load.
  - For Active/Standby: validate the standby region can serve **100%** of critical traffic (or define a documented degradation plan).
  - For Active/Active: validate each region can absorb an additional **+50–80%** burst depending on your steady-state split.
- **Autoscaling behavior:** Ensure scaling does not depend on impaired regional services (e.g., metrics pipeline in the same region).

### 2) Data residency and compliance constraints
- Define allowed failover destinations per tenant/workload.
- Confirm whether prompts, outputs, logs, and traces may cross borders.
- Ensure audit logging meets your requirements for “who changed steering and why.”

See: **Failover and Security Boundaries** (related page).

### 3) Networking and reachability
- Cross-region connectivity is validated for:
  - Client → gateway/entrypoint
  - Gateway → regional serving endpoints
  - Control plane dependencies (if centralized)
  - Any private peering (VPN/Interconnect) paths
- Synthetic probes exist and are monitored from at least two independent vantage points.

- Phase 0: Internal staging validation (eng + reliability): run synthetic regressions and iterate
  - Phase 1: Canary on 2% of hostnames with synthetic acceptance suite active for 30 minutes per cohort

safety lifecycle and signal-driven playbook that coordinates release blockers, abort/rollback decisioning, and templated communications across Product, Engineering, SRE, Design, Legal, and GTM. The playbook will be the canonical runbook used during the runtime-1.22 rollout and referenced in release notes and launch comms.

Scope and deliverables:
- Blocker taxonomy: agreed definitions (P0/P1/P2), examples (data loss, exposed PII, regression in latency beyond 2x baseline, sustained 5xx error rate >1% for 5m), and owner mapping.
- Abort/Abort-to-Rollback criteria: concrete metrics + time windows to trigger a halt (e.g., sustained QPS drop >30% with healthy instances, KV cache invalidation observed, or model output hallucination rate increase detected by eval probe).
- Rollback plan: fast rollback steps for hosted and dedicated deployments, staged rollback variants (soft-fallback to compatible model family, full rollback to prior release, capacity-based throttling), required runbook commands and automation hooks (GitHub PR labels -> CI/CD pipeline rollback job).
- Incident communications templates: internal incident summary, engineering postmortem stub, customer-facing status page updates, partner escalation email, and GTM-safe release note boilerplate. Each template includes placeholders for impact, ETA-to-fix, mitigation steps, and recommended customer guidance.
- Signal catalogue and dashboards: prioritized signals (latency p95, token cost delta, 5xx rate, per-route error rate, KV cache hit ratio, autoscaler saturation), owner for each signal, primary and secondary alert channels, and runbook links.
- Stakeholder roster and escalation ladder: primary owners (SRE, Runtime Eng, API Platform, Product), cross-team liaisons, on-call escalation levels, and executive notification criteria.
- Release-notes and GTM coordination checklist: owners for user-visible changes, review windows, embargo timelines, and legal/marketing sign-offs.
- Automation and enforcement: PR label conventions (release-blocker/rollback-required), preflight CI gates (smoke tests, canary traffic run), and automation tasks for Slack alert attachments and status

Description: Goal: Implement an escrowed activation flow that lets Optimize suggestions (batching/caching configs) be automatically proposed and partially enacted behind operator holdpoints. Each activation must include a replayable revert bundle so we can reliably roll back multi-part config changes across Dedicated and Private deployments. This ticket covers the orchestration layer, holdpoint API, approval signals, and the minimal safety checks required prior to progressive ramping.

Background: Optimize currently generates recommendations for batching and KV caching profiles. - Staged rollback contracts: For any runtime change affecting routing or model variant selection, a 3-stage rollout (canary 1%, regional ramp, global ramp) must be defined with explicit SLO thresholds; if 95th- or 99th-percentile latency or error-rate exceeds threshold for 5m in the canary stage, automated rollback triggers within 2m.
  - Synthetic canary harness: Implement a CI job that runs synthetic traffic (tail-latency and correctness prompts) against canary instances for every release; canary tests produce a pass/fail signal in CI and must be green before proceeding to ramp stage.
  - Telemetry gates: Dashboards (per-route, per-model) including latency P50/P95/P99, error-rate, token-cost delta, and KV-cache hit-rate must be auto-generated and declared green in the release checklist; ownership assigned to runtime-observability (ENG-22488).
  - Runbook integration: Rollback steps and escalation targets (SRE pager list, on-call runbook link) must be embedded in PRD; runbook must include isolation steps, diagnostic queries, and rollout-shepherd instructions for traffic shepherding and traffic pinning.
  - Test coverage: Add automated integration tests that simulate regional capacity loss and validate that staged rollback and fallback to compatible model variant works within acceptance latency bounds.
  - Audit & traceability: Every release that used staged rollback contracts must include a short post-release verification note with links to dashboards and Canary CI results; the PRD mandates storage of these artifacts for 90 days.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1: In staging, introducing a synthetic kernel regression (injecting a controlled latency penalty) must trigger the circuit-breaker within 3 minutes and route 100% of new requests to the fallback kernel within 5 minutes

  - AC6: End-to-end test that replays a recorded KV-cache regeneration pattern completes without data corruption and latency SLOs are preserved for >=95% of requests

## Rollout Plan

- Phase 0: Internal staging validation (eng + reliability): run synthetic regressions and iterate
  - Phase 1: Canary on 2% of hostnames with synthetic acceptance suite active for 30 minutes per cohort
  - Phase 2: Progressive ramp to 25% with additional automated checks and manual on-call sign-off

2) Mixed worker states after rollback
- Symptoms
  - Some workers report applied_version_id = old, others = target.
- Actions
  - Trigger reconciliation again (idempotent applier should converge).
  - If stuck, do a controlled rolling restart of the affected worker pool.
  - Verify you’re running the build that includes the apply/rollback race fix.

3) RBAC blocks rollback during incident
- Symptoms
  - 403/permission denied from API/CLI.
- Actions
  - Pre-provision break-glass role for on-call.
  - Validate the role in a staging environment (don’t wait for a Sev event).

4) “Version not found” during rollback
- Causes
  - Target version exists in hosted control plane but not in Private
  - Retention / migration issues
- Actions
  - Ensure the version was created/imported into the Private control plane.
  - Keep a catalog of known-good versions per deployment.

Section F — Change management recommendations (Private customers)
Minimum documentation per optimization change
- Scope (deployment/model/region)
- From version → to version
- Rationale (what you’re changing and why)
- Expected impact (latency/cost/quality)
- Canary plan + owner
- Rollback plan (target version, decision threshold)

Suggested canary pattern (Private)
- Create a separate canary scope if your topology supports it:
  - A small worker pool / nodepool
  - A dedicated region if multi-region
  - A dedicated tenant/environment
- Apply config to canary scope only
- Observe for 30–60 minutes under representative load
- Promote by switching active pointer for the main scope

Gate evaluation semantics: each gate returns pass/warn/fail. A single fail triggers auto-rollback when automation is enabled. Warns pause ramp and require manual approval to continue.

Instrumentation: Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, token generation time, 5xx counts, decode-fail counts, throughput, GPU memory/SM utilization.

Body: Summary:

This playbook defines a repeatable governance process to align product roadmaps with SLO commitments and capacity allocations. It codifies how feature teams request SLO changes, how SRE evaluates capacity impact, and how error-budget reconciliation is performed quarterly and on-demand. The goal is to reduce SLO drift, avoid surprise capacity shortfalls, and create clear tradeoffs between new feature delivery and reliability.

Scope:
- Applies to all externally visible latency and availability SLOs served by Redwood production clusters (hosted API, Dedicated control plane, and Private control plane proxies).
- Includes multi-tenant routing impacts, burst capacity commitments, and model onboarding windows.
- Does NOT cover internal-only metrics (developer tooling telemetry) unless they affect customer-facing SLAs.

Motivation and objectives:
- Provide an auditable process that links product roadmap milestones to capacity commitments and SLO changes.
- Ensure capacity procurement or reallocation decisions are taken with explicit error-budget risk assessment.
- Make tradeoffs explicit: for each new capability, either increase capacity, accept higher cost-per-token, or accept reduced SLO target for a bounded period.",

- Trigger: any event that consumes >50% of error budget in 24h or any P0 outage.

Operational Tooling Recommendations
- Capacity estimator: runcapacity --service <name> --window 14d --safety 0.3 (returns GPU-hours + suggested node types).

Rollout and Canary Guidelines
- Canary cadence: 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% with at least 30 minutes at each stage and SLO checks.
- Abort criteria: any canary stage that increases error burn rate by >3x baseline or produces >0.5% absolute drop in success rate.

2) Dedicated
- Purchase motion: contract/commit for reserved capacity
- Support expectations: faster response/update cadence than self-serve; explicit escalation triggers for capacity events
- Important distinction: Dedicated does not automatically mean 24x7 incident comms unless contracted.

3) Private
- Deployment: customer VPC/on-prem package (regulated workloads)
- Support expectations: stronger coordination + runbook-driven troubleshooting; sensitive info handling requirements
- Important distinction: Private may have customer-operated components; avoid language that implies Redwood controls all failure domains.

4) Enterprise (commercial tier overlay)
- “Enterprise” is not a deployment mode; it is a commercial/support package that may apply to Hosted, Dedicated, or Private.
- Recommendation: In docs, use “Enterprise Support” as an overlay label (e.g., “Hosted + Enterprise Support”, “Dedicated + Enterprise Support”).
- If we keep “enterprise” as a row in SLA tables, we need a footnote that it is a support package (coverage/targets) and may require contract verification.

Contract / legal language considerations (Sofia review required)
High-risk phrasing to avoid (or to qualify clearly)
- “Guaranteed”, “commit”, “will”, “ensure”, “24/7”, “real-time”, “immediate” when describing response/mitigation.
- “Status page updates every X minutes” as a guarantee. Approval flows and incident classification can prevent that.
- “Credits” language that suggests automatic entitlements.

Safer phrasing patterns
- Use “target”, “aim”, “typical”, “during coverage hours”, “best-effort outside coverage hours unless contracted”.
- Separate: (A) first response targets, (B) update cadence targets while actively investigating, (C) escalation triggers (when we page Engineering/on-call).

- SLO: Service Level Objective (target value for an SLI over a rolling window).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO over the evaluation window (commonly 28 days).
- Steward: individual responsible for SLO health, runbook updates, and coordination.

SLO Taxonomy and Examples
Use this taxonomy when negotiating:
- Latency SLOs (user-facing): p50/p95/p99 tail per route, measured at ingress after auth.
- Availability SLOs (success rate): 5xx+4xx-excluding-rate-limited / total requests.
- Correctness SLOs (quality): task-specific metric, e.g., regression against verified prompt set (for core models).
- Cost-awareness indicators: tokens-per-request and mean GPU-ms per request (inform capacity reservations).

Example baseline commitments (starting point for negotiations):
- Hosted-generation-default: p95 <= 350ms, success >= 99.5% (28d), error budget 0.5%.
- Large-context-chat: p95 <= 800ms, success >= 99.0% (28d), error budget 1.0%.
- Embeddings-batch: p95 <= 1200ms, success >= 99.8% (28d), error budget 0.2%.
(These are examples — negotiate per-tenant when needed.)

Incident Review Standards (brief)
- Trigger: any event that consumes >50% of error budget in 24h or any P0 outage.

- Capacity estimator: runcapacity --service <name> --window 14d --safety 0.3 (returns GPU-hours + suggested node types).

Rollout and Canary Guidelines
- Canary cadence: 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% with at least 30 minutes at each stage and SLO checks.
- Abort criteria: any canary stage that increases error burn rate by >3x baseline or produces >0.5% absolute drop in success rate.

Purpose: This document defines how we curate runbooks, assign incident ownership, and standardize on-call rotations, game-day exercises, postmortem output, and customer status templates. Key definitions

This document is a curated catalog of realistic runtime rollback scenarios for the Redwood serving platform, paired with a deterministic SLO impact mapping and step-by-step operator checklists. ----------------
- Rollbacks are common and high-risk; ad-hoc decisions increase blast radius.
- Quantifying SLO impact for each rollback path reduces decision inertia.
- Standardized checklists reduce operator cognitive load during high-severity events.

Owners and stakeholders
-----------------------
- Primary owner: Platform SRE (team: eng-platform)

     - Check service health endpoints: curl -fsS https://platform-monitoring/_health || true\     - Query per-route P95: curl -s 'https://metrics/api?series=route_latency.p95&route=...'
     - Inspect queue depths, backpressure, GPU utilization (nvidia-smi wrapper): /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-util.sh --list
   - Apply containment: scale up worker pool, enable degraded model variant, or enable rate-limiting exemptions. Prefer non-destructive steps first.
3) Mitigation and recovery\   - Work with service owner to apply a controlled mitigation (examples below).\   - Validate recovery by observing: request success rate >98% and P95 latency within SLO for 10 continuous minutes.\   - If mitigation fails, escalate to cross-team bridge and consider traffic diversion or rollback.
4) Customer communications\   - Communications lead posts an initial internal incident note within 10 minutes and crafts customer-facing status messages (templates below).
5) Post-incident review\   - IC assigns a postmortem owner and ensures the postmortem is published within 72 hours.

Content: Overview

Purpose: This document defines how we curate runbooks, assign incident ownership, and standardize on-call rotations, game-day exercises, postmortem output, and customer status templates. It establishes a lifecycle for runbooks (creation → review → retirement), a lightweight incident command ladder, and concrete communication templates for status page and customer notices.

Audience: on-call engineers, SREs, service owners, people-ops, and incident commanders.

Key definitions

- Service owner: team and primary engineer responsible for the long-term health of a service (maintenance, SLOs, runbooks).
- Incident commander (IC): temporary owner of incident coordination until handoff.
- Operator / responder: engineer executing runbooks.
- Runbook steward: person responsible for keeping runbooks accurate and up-to-date.

Runbook lifecycle and governance

1) Creation (initial authoring)
- Required fields for each runbook: title, service, primary steward, last-reviewed, related playbooks, severity tiers covered, prerequisites, immediate containment steps, and post-incident tasks.
- Add a short summary line at the top: single-sentence intended use.
- Naming convention: service-action-severity (e.g., runtime-prefix-eviction-P1).

Content: Summary
-------
This document is a curated catalog of realistic runtime rollback scenarios for the Redwood serving platform, paired with a deterministic SLO impact mapping and step-by-step operator checklists. It is written for platform operators, oncall engineers, and SREs to improve response consistency, speed, and post-incident learning.

Scope
-----
- Applicable systems: inference runtime (request router, batching layer, KV prefix cache), model variant service, compiler/kernel selector, regional allocator, and prefetch coordinator.
- Not covered: billing reconciliation, legal/compliance notifications, or customer-facing postmortem text (see escalation-playbook).

Why this exists
----------------
- Rollbacks are common and high-risk; ad-hoc decisions increase blast radius.
- Quantifying SLO impact for each rollback path reduces decision inertia.
- Standardized checklists reduce operator cognitive load during high-severity events.

Owners and stakeholders
-----------------------
- Primary owner: Platform SRE (team: eng-platform)
- Runtime product owner: Runtime Team (eng-serving-runtime)
- Oncall escalation: Platform oncall -> Runtime oncall -> Incident Commander
- Communications: Customer Success for enterprise customers, Growth for self-serve anomalies

Minimum evidence artifacts:
- Change ticket or incident record.
- A short timeline with key timestamps.
- Links/screenshots to dashboards showing trigger signals.
- A record of steering configuration before/after.

## Roles and escalation (suggested)
Define these roles for your organization; names vary by customer.
- **Incident Commander (IC):** owns decision-making and comms.
- **Traffic/Networking Operator:** executes steering changes.
- **Platform Operator:** validates capacity, scaling, and serving health.
- **Security/Compliance approver:** if cross-region boundaries may be impacted.

Redwood escalation (typical)
- Private deployments on-call: first responder for Redwood component health.
- If network reachability is implicated: coordinate with customer network team and Redwood Network (Victor Alvarez) as needed.
- If control plane changes are required: involve Control Plane lead (Ethan Park) via support escalation.

## FAQ
### Can Redwood automatically fail over my Private deployment like Hosted API?
Not by default. Hosted/Dedicated automation relies on Redwood-owned routing and standardized telemetry/control channels. Private environments require customer-specific integration, approvals, and security boundaries.

### What is the safest “first step” to multi-region?
Active/Standby with controlled drills, conservative triggers, and explicit failback. Most incidents are made worse by premature failback and retry storms.

### Do we need cross-region data replication for inference?
It depends on what state you maintain outside Redwood serving. Stateless inference can often fail over without state replication, but audit logs, request logs, caches, and any customer application state may require replication or careful scoping.

## Change log
- 2026-02-12: Clarified support models (customer-managed vs Redwood-assisted), added streaming and retry caveats, and standardized trigger hierarchy language to match Reliability Program guidance.
- 2026-01-27: Initial published version.

evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:
- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)
- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated
- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)

**Drain** means: stop placing new work on a pool and let in-flight work complete (or age out) while routing shifts traffic elsewhere.

**Evacuation** means: drain + expedite termination/migration of remaining workloads (with stricter safeguards), typically when the region is actively failing.

This procedure must be coordinated with routing (policy engine + failover controller) to avoid creating a thundering herd, retry storms, or overload in the target region.

---

## Scope / ownership
**Applies to:**
- Hosted API serving GPU pools (multi-tenant)
- Dedicated customer pools (tenant-isolated)

**Not covered:**
- Customer-managed on-prem clusters (see Private deployment guidance)

**Primary on-call:** Infra (Fleet/Capacity) + SRE

**Key coordination roles:**
- SRE on-call (incident commander / traffic shift approvals)
- Routing/control plane on-call (policy flips, hold-down/rollback)
- Network on-call (reachability validation)
- Dedicated support liaison (customer notifications when required)

---

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when **any** of the following is true:
1) Failover controller recommends or executes regional failover and indicates **pool drain required**.
2) Region health is **UNHEALTHY** (reachability authoritative) and continuing to accept new requests will increase customer impact.
3) GPU pool shows sustained symptoms consistent with regional impairment:
   - Elevated 5xx burn rate + corroborated reachability failures
   - Severe tail latency burn with network symptoms
   - Control plane errors impacting scheduling/placement
4) Planned controlled failover test (game day) includes pool drain/evacuation steps.

- Phase 0 - Detection: Confirm cross-region scope using global latency dashboard, p95/p99 error heatmap, and dedicated pool telemetry (GPU OOMs, scheduling failures). Use tag 'cross-region' in the incident room.
  - Phase 1 - Containment: If two or more regions show sustained p95 > 2x baseline AND error rate increase > 3x, initiate cross-region failover protocol.
  - Phase 2 - Traffic Shift Preparation: Verify capacity in candidate target region (available GPU slots, model variant compatibility, matching quantization profiles). Check KV cache hit rate history and plan for warmup time (estimate warmup RTT per prefix).
  - Phase 3 - Traffic Shift Execution (manual steps):
  -   1) Enter maintenance window in Console for affected routes and pause background billing-heavy tasks for dedicated customers as needed.
  -   2) Adjust Smart Routing weights: set primary region weight to 0.1 and target region to 0.9 in increments (0 -> 10% -> 50% -> 90%) with 2 minute observation between steps.
  -   3) If using DNS-based mitigation, ensure global LB TTL <= 60s before initiating. Prefer global LB weight updates over DNS for lower lead time.
  -   4) Warm KV caches via /internal/cache-warm for top 200 prefixes and run a controlled synthetic load at 5-10% of production RPS to pre-fill caches.
  -   5) Validate functional correctness: run smoke tests (generation, chat, embeddings) against target region and compare outputs against golden prompts (allowing model-variant deltas).
  - Phase 4 - Post-shift Validation: Monitor p50/p95/p99 latency, error rates, and client-side observed timeouts for 30 minutes at steady traffic. Ensure SLOs return to acceptable thresholds. If regression observed, revert weights by 50% or fall back to canary route.
  - Phase 5 - Rollback Criteria: Define automatic rollback triggers: sustained >15% error rate increase, p99 > 3x baseline

signals triggered it?

Minimum evidence artifacts:
- Change ticket or incident record.
- A short timeline with key timestamps.
- Links/screenshots to dashboards showing trigger signals.
- A record of steering configuration before/after.

## Roles and escalation (suggested)
Define these roles for your organization; names vary by customer.
- **Incident Commander (IC):** owns decision-making and comms.
- **Traffic/Networking Operator:** executes steering changes.
- **Platform Operator:** validates capacity, scaling, and serving health.
- **Security/Compliance approver:** if cross-region boundaries may be impacted.

Redwood escalation (typical)
- Private deployments on-call: first responder for Redwood component health.
- If network reachability is implicated: coordinate with customer network team and Redwood Network (Victor Alvarez) as needed.
- If control plane changes are required: involve Control Plane lead (Ethan Park) via support escalation.

## FAQ
### Can Redwood automatically fail over my Private deployment like Hosted API?
Not by default. Hosted/Dedicated automation relies on Redwood-owned routing and standardized telemetry/control channels. Private environments require customer-specific integration, approvals, and security boundaries.

### What is the safest “first step” to multi-region?
Active/Standby with controlled drills, conservative triggers, and explicit failback. Most incidents are made worse by premature failback and retry storms.

### Do we need cross-region data replication for inference?
It depends on what state you maintain outside Redwood serving. Stateless inference can often fail over without state replication, but audit logs, request logs, caches, and any customer application state may require replication or careful scoping.

## Change log
- 2026-02-12: Clarified support models (customer-managed vs Redwood-assisted), added streaming and retry caveats, and standardized trigger hierarchy language to match Reliability Program guidance.

Title: GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)

evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:
- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)
- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated
- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)

**Drain** means: stop placing new work on a pool and let in-flight work complete (or age out) while routing shifts traffic elsewhere.

**Evacuation** means: drain + expedite termination/migration of remaining workloads (with stricter safeguards), typically when the region is actively failing.

This procedure must be coordinated with routing (policy engine + failover controller) to avoid creating a thundering herd, retry storms, or overload in the target region.

---

## Scope / ownership
**Applies to:**
- Hosted API serving GPU pools (multi-tenant)
- Dedicated customer pools (tenant-isolated)

**Not covered:**
- Customer-managed on-prem clusters (see Private deployment guidance)

**Primary on-call:** Infra (Fleet/Capacity) + SRE

**Key coordination roles:**
- SRE on-call (incident commander / traffic shift approvals)
- Routing/control plane on-call (policy flips, hold-down/rollback)
- Network on-call (reachability validation)
- Dedicated support liaison (customer notifications when required)

---

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when **any** of the following is true:
1) Failover controller recommends or executes regional failover and indicates **pool drain required**.
2) Region health is **UNHEALTHY** (reachability authoritative) and continuing to accept new requests will increase customer impact.
3) GPU pool shows sustained symptoms consistent with regional impairment:
   - Elevated 5xx burn rate + corroborated reachability failures
   - Severe tail latency burn with network symptoms
   - Control plane errors impacting scheduling/placement
4) Planned controlled failover test (game day) includes pool drain/evacuation steps.

---

LTSs in release notes and include a compatibility matrix artifact. SDKs must pass end-to-end regression tests against the runtime test harness gated in CI before release to LTS channel.
- Console: supports current LTS and previous LTS for dashboards and runtime control plane. Non-LTS feature flags may be hidden unless explicitly enabled.

Rollout gates and observability-driven promotion:
- Staging -> Canary (1%) -> Canary (10%) -> Progressive (50%) -> Wide (100%). Each step gated by automated checks over a 4-hour window: error rate (5xx delta threshold), p99 latency, token-generation correctness (synthetic prompts and eval prompts), SDK and API contract regressions, and customer-visible metric anomalies.
- Gate thresholds: default trigger if error-rate delta > 1.5x baseline or p99 latency increase > 20% sustained for 15 minutes. For high-risk builds (runtime or kernel changes), require additional safety: manual signoff from SRE and applied chaos test run.
- Automatic rollback: if any gate fails or there is a sudden increase in error-rate/latency, rollback to the previous stable LTS-compatible image and create an incident with a predefined runbook.

Upgrade tooling & workflows:
- Migration CLI (redwood-upgrade): assists Dedicated/Private customers to evaluate their cluster, run preflight checks, and apply staged upgrades. Outputs a compatibility report mapping installed SDKs and third-party integrations to required versions.
- In-hosted pathing: Hosted customers can pin to an LTS channel; platform will offer a one-click upgrade flow that runs synthetic checks and schedules the migration window per customer.
- CI integration: Add release-checker job that runs SDK matrix tests against runtime LTS images and publishes a compatibility artifact (JSON) that the Console and SDK package releases consume.

D (limited external customers + docs): opt-in customers on Dedicated + Hosted beta.
Canary schedule defaults: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with wait windows 10m, 20m, 30m, 1h (configurable).

Gates: We will provide a set of preconfigured gates and allow custom metric expressions:
- Latency Gate: p95 increase <= 15% relative to baseline over gate window (default 15m).
- Error Gate: request 5xx rate <= baseline + 0.2% absolute (sliding 15m).
- Decode Failure Gate: any spike > 3x baseline triggers immediate fail.
- Quality Gate: evaluated by running 200 golden prompts against new and baseline models and checking BLEU/ROUGE/semantic-similarity delta; fail if quality drops > configured delta (default 2%).
- Resource Gate: GPU memory pressure > 80% sustained for 5m causes pause.
Gate evaluation semantics: each gate returns pass/warn/fail. A single fail triggers auto-rollback when automation is enabled. Warns pause ramp and require manual approval to continue.

Instrumentation: Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, token generation time, 5xx counts, decode-fail counts, throughput, GPU memory/SM utilization.
Tracing: attach request-level traces to canary samples.
Logs: structured audit events for start/step/fail/rollback with controller run_id.
Synthetic checks: small harness that hits both new and baseline variants in parallel for golden prompts.
Dashboards: per-rollout timeline with gate status, metric deltas, and decision timestamps.
PRs and contracts: routing-api PR (github.com/redwood/re-routing/pulls/212), controller proto (github.com/redwood/re-release/pulls/37).

Objective: Produce a supported-versions matrix that explicitly defines allowed version skew and behavioral contracts between runtime, API, SDKs, and console; deliver a prototype orchestrator that runs preflight validations, performs canary cohort promotions, and executes safe rollbacks based on SLO and functional checks.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Compatibility map document completed and reviewed by Runtime, API, SDK, and Console leads
  - Allowed version skew rules defined for each surface and encoded as machine-readable policies
  - Prototype silent-upgrade orchestrator can run a staged upgrade: canary (5%), ramp (25%), full rollout with automated rollback on defined failure signals
  - Preflight suite of compatibility tests (contract, end-to-end smoke, KV-cache replay) integrated into orchestrator and passing in CI for target minor-version pairs
  - Runbook and rollback playbook documented and linked from Console release page
  - Small-scale private deployment upgrade executed in staging with no customer-facing errors and post-upgrade metrics within SLOs

## Rollout Gates

- Preflight: contract checks (OpenAPI/protobuf), semantic schema diffs, SDK surface diff reports
  - Performance smoke: 95th percentile token latency within 1.5x baseline for a representative workload
  - Behavioral smoke: 20 canonical prompt/eval set pass rate within 98% of baseline
  - Observability: tracing and token-level cost events are present and mapped to new runtime version
  - Canary cohort: 5% of traffic for 2 hours with anomaly detection (error rate, latency, quality metrics), manual approval if anomalies are ambiguous
  - Ramp gate: automatic step-up to 25% then 100% if no gate breaches; each step requires at least 30 minutes of stable telemetry
  - Rollback triggers: sustained error rate > 0.5% above baseline for 5 minutes OR quality regression > 2% on canonical evals OR severe latency spike beyond configured SLO breach

Description: Build a drift-aware progressive delivery framework for runtime upgrades and model version promotions. Goals: minimize user-visible regressions, enforce LTS compatibility rules, reduce manual toil for canaries and rollbacks, and introduce automated fallback paths when runtime or model drift is detected. The scope covers: - version compatibility checks (binary, weights, KV cache schema) - staged traffic ramps with adaptive gates driven by telemetry - canary cohorts, shadowing and mirrored traffic modes - feature-flag driven opt-in/out and emergency kill-switch - automatic rollback policies tied to SLO/quality gates - tooling to declare LTS channels and safe upgrade windows

Rollout Plan Summary: 1) Preflight: run compatibility checks and smoke-tests on preprod cluster; 2) Canary: route 0.5% traffic to canary cohort for 10 minutes with full tracing; 3) Adaptive ramp: increase to 5%, 20%, 50% using telemetry gates (latency p95, error rate, quality delta); 4) Final cutover: promote to LTS channel if all gates green; 5) Auto-rollback: trigger immediate fallback if any critical gate trips; 6) Post-mortem: automated artifact collection and release note generation.

Body: Summary
This playbook describes a field-operator-centric on-call and incident response program focused on readiness, evidence collection for SLA/regulatory requests, and repeatable game-day rehearsals. It is intended for SREs, service owners, and first-responders who operate Redwood inference runtime services.

Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing inference services (hosted API routes, dedicated pools, private control plane bridges).
- Covers incidents that cause SLO degradations (latency, availability, correctness) or require customer comms.
- This document does not replace service-specific runbooks; it supplements them with readiness and evidence templates.

Goals
1. Ensure responders can stabilize incidents within 10 minutes for P1 latency regressions and 60 minutes for regional outages (see SLO thresholds).
2. Provide a standardized evidence package (timeline, metrics, snapshots, logs) for SLA calculations and regulatory audits within 48 hours.
3. Make game-day rehearsals repeatable with measurable skills and a triage scoring rubric.

- **Recording rules and aggregation strategy** must avoid cardinality explosion while preserving actionable breakdowns (tier, endpoint class, region; limited “top-N” model/route views).
- **SLO config schema** must support tier/region/endpoint scoping and be validated in CI.

### Process dependencies
- Agreement with Product on:
  - Which SLOs are internal-only vs shareable for Dedicated reporting.
  - Which exclusions are appropriate for customer-facing SLAs.
- Updated incident process tying burn-rate to incident classification and comms requirements.

---

## Enforcement model (phased)
This program intentionally stages enforcement to avoid blocking critical reliability fixes early on.

1) **Visibility first** (dashboards + annotations)
- SLO dashboards available for Hosted and Dedicated.
- Deploy and incident annotations visible on SLO timelines.

2) **Alerting** (multi-window burn-rate)
- Burn-rate alerts page correct rotations.
- Alerts link directly to dashboards, traces, and mitigation runbooks.

3) **Warn-only gates**
- CI/CD checks evaluate current error budget state.
- Gate posts warnings (Slack + deploy output) and logs any overrides.

4) **Enforced gates**
- When a tier is in a red state (budget exhausted or acute burn), block non-emergency deploys.
- Emergency fixes permitted via explicit override procedure with audit trail.

---

## Graceful degradation (expectations by tier)
We will document tier-specific behavior and ensure SLI accounting aligns with user impact.

**Hosted (shared):**
- Prefer platform stability under overload: bounded queues, overload shedding, and controlled fallback to compatible variants.
- Expect more aggressive protective measures (rate limiting, load shedding) to protect shared infrastructure.

**Dedicated:**
- Prioritize predictability: capacity headroom commitments, fast mitigation via fleet actions, and conservative fallback policies.
- Customer-specific dashboards and incident comms should reflect dedicated impact separately from Hosted.

document.title: project list
document.content:
# Serving Runtime Performance (Kernel + Scheduling)
Perf baseline & representative workload suite: Establish Q1 2026 latency/throughput baselines across top models and traffic shapes.
Mixed-workload scheduler prototype: Implement and test a short/long prompt scheduling policy to reduce p95 tail latency.
Kernel auto-selection v2 implementation: Ship improved kernel selection logic keyed on model family, seq length, and GPU type.
KV cache compaction improvements: Add compaction/eviction strategy to reduce memory fragmentation and burst tail latencies.
FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint: Benchmark quantization-friendly kernels on the top hosted models and GPUs.
Multi-GPU (TP) stability fixes: Fix known runtime hangs/timeouts in tensor-parallel execution under load.
Perf regression canary in prod: Deploy a small perf canary that alerts on p95 latency/tokens/sec regressions per model.
Hardware tuning profiles pack: Create tuned configs for H100/B200/L40S (or current fleet) and document expected behavior.
Runtime LTS branch & release process: Stand up an enterprise LTS channel with slower-change release notes and backport policy.

# Cost Optimization Automation (Batching, Caching, Quantization Profiles)
Internal unit economics dashboard: Build a dashboard for blended $/1M output tokens with drilldowns by model/region/customer tier.
Standard cost model spec + API: Define the cost model inputs/outputs and expose it to Console/Optimize services.
Optimization suggestions Console UX (beta): Add a “suggestions” view for batching/caching with estimated savings and risk level.
Safe apply + rollback mechanism: Implement config versioning plus one-click rollback for optimization changes.
Workload-aware batching defaults: Ship recommended batching profiles for common latency SLO tiers (fast/standard/cost-efficient).
Cache hit-rate instrumentation sprint: Improve prefix/KV cache telemetry and generate actionable “increase hit-rate” recommendations.
Quantization profile library (opt-in): Publish per-model quantization profiles with route-level enablement controls.
Quality guardrails gating for optimize: Require eval checks and regression thresholds before applying cost-saving config changes.

# Reliability Program (SLOs, Incident Reduction, Graceful Degradation)
Tiered SLO definitions + error budget policy: Define availability/latency/error SLOs per Hosted/Dedicated tier and enforce error budgets.
Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping: Classify top incident types and assign primary owners and remediation SLAs.
Regional failover automation upgrade: Improve region failover triggers and validate with controlled failover tests.
Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding: Add overload protection with clear customer-facing errors and safe degradation modes.
Hot-route capacity protection: Add rate-limit/quotas/priority routing for top enterprise routes to prevent fleet-wide impact.
Status page transparency upgrades: Improve component granularity, incident comms templates, and post-incident summaries.
Incident bot + diagnostics improvements: Enhance automated context gathering (recent deploys, config diffs, saturation signals).

# Unified Rollouts, A/B Testing, and Model Lifecycle
Model metadata schema + changelog generator: Standardize model/version metadata and auto-generate customer-visible release notes.
Hosted canary rollout workflow (GA): Ship canary UI + policy controls for percentage-based rollouts on Hosted routes.
Auto-rollback on SLO breach integration: Wire rollout controller to latency/error SLO monitors with configurable rollback thresholds.
Shadow traffic tool for eval metrics: Enable shadow testing and capture quality metrics without impacting user responses.
Route-level A/B testing framework: Support A/B splits with measurement hooks (latency, cost, eval scores) in Console.
Dedicated staged rollouts for reserved pools: Implement phased rollout controls for Dedicated capacity pools with per-stage gates.

# Enterprise Security & Compliance Foundation
RBAC v2 design + permission inventory: Inventory sensitive actions and implement fine-grained roles and permission checks.
Audit log schema standardization + coverage: Standardize event schema and ensure 100% coverage for sensitive actions.
SIEM-ready audit export (beta): Deliver export integration (e.g., Splunk/Datadog/S3) with filtering and delivery guarantees.
KMS integration hardening + rotation docs: Improve key handling, rotation procedures, and failure-mode testing.
Hosted data residency enforcement: Add region pinning with enforcement checks and clear error messaging for violations.
Retention controls + compliance reporting pack: Implement retention configuration and produce a baseline compliance report package.

# Private Deployment Automation (VPC + On-Prem Packaging)
VPC Terraform modules (alpha): Publish reference Terraform modules for standard VPC deployments with validated defaults.
Private observability minimum pack: Deliver baseline dashboards/alerts/log pipelines required for “supported” Private installs.
Private upgrade + rollback mechanism: Implement reliable upgrade workflow with prechecks, backups, and rollback hooks.
On-prem offline artifact signing: Add signed offline bundles and verification steps for air-gapped installs.
Day-2 ops toolkit (backup/restore): Provide documented scripts and runbooks for backup/restore and disaster recovery.

# Dedicated Capacity & Fleet Management
Dedicated throughput SLO + tier definitions: Define throughput guarantees and map to hardware shapes and pricing tiers.
Burst capacity option implementation: Add controlled burst pools with guardrails to protect neighbor workloads.

    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Dependability Compass \\u2014 cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability\",\n  \"owner\": \"Ethan Park\",\n  \"drive_area\": \"shared_drives\",\n  \"path\": \"shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering\",\n  \"doc_type\": \"doc\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-06-18\",\n  \"last_modified\": \"2026-07-02\",\n  \"collaborators\": [\n    \"Aisha Patel\",\n    \"Mariana Gomez\",\n    \"Ravi Kapoor\",\n    \"Lina Zhou\"\n  ],\n  \"team\": \"eng-sre\",\n  \"status\": \"in_review\",\n  \"tags\": [\n    \"dependability\",\n    \"playmap\",\n    \"model-serving\",\n    \"slo\",\n    \"canary\",\n    \"runbook\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_artifacts\": [\n    \"CONFLUENCE-REL/Dependability-Compass\",\n    \"JIRA-REL-517\",\n    \"github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/884\",\n    \"slack:#sre-ops\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"WORKING DRAFT \\u2014 Dependability Compass: cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability\\n\\nPurpose and context:\\n- This doc captures a concrete cross-functional plan to operationalize reliability goals for model-serving surfaces (hosted API, dedicated, private).\\n- Focus: translate product-level availability and correctness expectations into measurable signals, ownership, integration tasks, and a pragmatic rollout path that minimizes customer impact while improving long-term observability and remediation speed.\\n- Audience: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, Observability, Product-Hosted-API, Solutions Eng, Support.\\n\\nHigh-level objectives (what success looks like):\\n1) Observable, actionable signals for the top three failure modes across model-serving (model-load failures, KV cache regressions, tail-latency spikes).\\n2) Clear ownership and runbooks for each signal with measurable reduction targets in MTTD/MTTR over rolling 90-day windows.\\n3) A staged SLO adoption pattern that lets teams opt into strict error/latency targets with canary rollouts and automated fallback policies.\\n4) Two pilot services on dedicated infra with full pipeline (dashboards, alerts, automated rollback) within Q3 2026.\\n\\nGuiding principles:\\n- Incremental: instrument first, then set targets, then automate responses.\\n- Customer-impact focused: prioritize signals that map to user-visible degradation.\\n- Low blast radius: use progressive rollout (canary, cohort) for any enforcement.\\n- Cross-team pairing: each milestone requires an SRE + owning-engineer co-shipper.\\n\\nScope (in):\\n- Model-serving control plane and inference runtime path (request ingress, KV cache, model weights load, token generation latency).\\n- Observability (metrics, traces, logs) and alerting pipelines used by SRE and product teams.\\n- Runbooks and automated remediation playbooks.\\n\\nOut of scope (for this phase):\\n- Deep model quality evaluation (LLM hallucination metrics) \\u2014 covered by Optimize/product.\\n- Billing/charging changes for customers.\\n\\nStakeholders and lightweight RACI:\\n- Eng-SRE (lead): monitoring, alerting, runbooks, incident postmortem cadence \\u2014 R\\n- Serving Runtime: implementation of instrumentation, fallback hooks, canary flags \\u2014 A\\n- Observability: dashboards, trace sampling, log retention settings \\u2014 C\\n- Platform Engineering: infra capacity policies, autoscaling safety nets \\u2014 C\\n- Product-Hosted-API: product SLO definition & customer-facing comms \\u2014 I\\n- Solutions Eng / Support: pilot adoption and customer escalation play \\u2014 C\\n(Notes: R=Responsible, A=Accountable, C=Consulted, I=Informed)\\n\\nSignals, tentative metrics and starter targets (provisional \\u2014 iterate after telemetry baseline):\\n- Request Success Rate (5xx + model-load errors): baseline measurement window = 14d; pilot SLO target = 99.7% per 30d for non-burst endpoints.\\n- 95th/99th token-latency for inference: capture per-model and per-route; pilot latency SLO = 95th <= 300ms on fast-models, 99th <= 750ms.\\n- Model load latency and success (artifact fetch / weight deserialization): target = 99.9% successful within 15s.\\n- KV cache hit ratio and tail latency impact: signal only for services opting into KV caching; target: maintain degradation <10% customer impact during cache warmups.\\n\\nMonitoring & alerting pattern:\\n- Three alert tiers: WARNING (signal trending bad), INCIDENT (customer-impacting degradation), OUTAGE (SLA violation imminent or occurring).\\n- Use metric-derived anomaly windows + heatmap of errors by region/model to reduce noisy pager noise.\\n- Attach runbook link in alert payload; require initial triage within 10 minutes for INCIDENT.\\n\\nRunbooks and automation (practical examples):\\n- Runbook: high 5xx rate from a model-serving pod: steps \\u2014 1) check model-weight load errors, 2) check OOMs, 3) scale down circuit-breaker, 4) failover to model-variant v2 with pinned weights, 5) engage fallback routing.\\n- Automation: when model-load errors > threshold on 3 hosts in 5m, automatically mark model variant as degraded and route new requests to fallback pool. Manual approval required before re-enable.\\n\\nCanary and rollout pattern (phase gates):\\nPhase 0 (instrument + baseline) \\u2014 3 weeks\\n- Implement key metrics and traces for pilot services. Pair SRE + runtime eng.\\n- Build dashboard templates and export baseline numbers.\\n\\nPhase 1 (soft SLOs + runbooks) \\u2014 4 weeks\\n- Publish soft SLO targets (non-punitive) and runbooks.\\n- Run canaries on internal traffic only.\\n\\nPhase 2 (automated fallback + guarded SLOs) \\u2014 6 weeks\\n- Add automated fallback policy for the most common failure (model-load).\\n- Start rolling SLOs to small customer cohorts behind a feature flag.\\n\\nPhase 3 (broader enforcement) \\u2014 6\\u20138 weeks\\n- Expand enforcement, ensure platform controls prevent noisy autoscale oscillations.\\n- Complete postmortem playbooks and SLO reporting.\\n\\nSprint-by-sprint starter backlog (first 8 sprints, two-week sprints assumed):\\nSprint 1: metrics schema, instrumentation hooks merged, dashboard skeletons, export baseline script.\\nSprint 2: alert definitions (warning/incident/outage), basic runbook drafts, link to oncall rotation.\\nSprint 3: implement canary flag, traffic routing for canary, label propagation for traces.\\nSprint 4: automation prototype for model-load fallback, test harness for rollback.\\nSprint 5: pilot on Dedicated infra (two services), SRE-led chaos runbook validation.\\nSprint 6: telemetry-driven SLO adjustments, comms template for customers.\\nSprint 7: scaling safety-net work (platform autoscale playbooks), cost-impact review.\\nSprint 8: finalize runbooks, production rollouts for cohort A, dashboarding for exec summary.\\n\\nCross-team dependency map (key dependencies that block progress):\\n- Serving Runtime needs to expose model load/error tags and a per-request model-variant identifier. Blocker: missing tagging per request.\\n- Observability needs to add a low-cost trace sampling policy and retention for 30d for pilot metrics. Blocker: retention quota limits in prod logging account.\\n- Platform must provide dedicated canary pools and feature-flag gating for traffic split. Blocker: infra quotas for dedicated GPUs.\\n\\nRisk register & mitigation notes:\\n- Risk: Alert fatigue causing ignored incidents. Mitigation: implement signal aggregation and reduce noisy low-value alerts before escalations.\\n- Risk: Fallback policies mask underlying reliability problems. Mitigation: ensure fallback triggers incident creation and postmortem requirement.\\n- Risk: Costs from additional telemetry and retention. Mitigation: use targeted sampling and short retention for verbose traces; keep metrics high-level.\\n\\nCustomer communications and escalations:\\n- For pilots: proactive notice to pilot customers outlining expected maintenance windows and rollback behavior.\\n- For broader rollouts: staged emails + in-console banner with opt-out for early customers.\\n- Support play: Solutions Eng to own first-line customer comms, SRE to own technical explanation and remediation timeline.\\n\\nOpen questions (to be resolved in the next working sync):\\n- Which product routes should be in the initial two pilot services? proposal: text-generation (low-latency path) + embeddings (throughput path).\\n- What is acceptable cost delta for adding trace retention for pilot services? target: <10% increase in observability bill for pilot.\\n- How do we align model-variant pinning semantics across hosted and private customers? need design doc from Serving Runtime.\\n\\nNext immediate actions (owners + due dates):\\n- Ethan Park: create dashboard templates and baseline export job \\u2014 due 2026-06-25.\\n- Aisha Patel: draft runbook templates and run triage play \\u2014 due 2026-06-28.\\n- Mariano Gomez: (Observability) propose sampling/retention plan \\u2014 due 2026-06-30.\\n- Ravi Kapoor: check infra quotas for canary pools and report blockers \\u2014 due 2026-07-02.\\n\\nAppendix: notes for pairing sessions and quick checklists\\n- Pairing rule: every change that affects an alert or runbook must have at least one SRE reviewer and one owning-service reviewer.\\n- Quick triage checklist for oncall: always record first-action timestamp, whether automatic fallback executed, and whether customer impact (yes/no).\\n\\nNotes to reviewers:\\n- This is intentionally prescriptive at the tactical level to get cross-team alignment quickly. Expect adjustments to SLO targets after we ingest baseline telemetry.\\n- Please comment on the proposed pilot services and add any missing failure modes you\\u2019ve observed in the past 6 months.\\n\\nEnd of document.\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_57af13fe38eb4113b6e6083f571ecff9\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Dependability Compass — cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/dependability-compass-cross-team-playmap.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: eng-sre\n\nFocus: translate product-level availability and correctness expectations into measurable signals, ownership, integration tasks, and a pragmatic rollout path that minimizes customer impact while improving long-term observability and remediation speed.\n- Audience: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, Observability, Product-Hosted-API, Solutions Eng, Support.\n\nHigh-level objectives (what success looks like):\n1) Observable, actionable signals for the top three failure modes across model-serving (model-load failures, KV cache regressions, tail-latency spikes).\n2) Clear ownership and runbooks for each signal with measurable reduction targets in MTTD/MTTR over rolling 90-day windows.\n3) A staged SLO adoption pattern that lets teams opt into strict error/latency targets with canary rollouts and automated fallback policies.\n4) Two pilot services on dedicated infra with full pipeline (dashboards, alerts, automated rollback) within Q3 2026.\n\nGuiding principles:\n- Incremental: instrument first, then set targets, then automate responses.\n- Customer-impact focused: prioritize signals that map to user-visible degradation.\n- Low blast radius: use progressive rollout (canary, cohort) for any enforcement.\n- Cross-team pairing: each milestone requires an SRE + owning-engineer co-shipper.\n\nScope (in):\n- Model-serving control plane and inference runtime path (request ingress, KV cache, model weights load, token generation latency).\n- Observability (metrics, traces, logs) and alerting pipelines used by SRE and product teams.\n- Runbooks and automated remediation playbooks.\n\nOut of scope (for this phase):\n- Deep model quality evaluation (LLM hallucination metrics) — covered by Optimize/product.\n- Billing/charging changes for customers.",
