      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Dependability Compass — cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/dependability-compass-cross-team-playmap.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: eng-sre\n\nmetrics, traces, logs) and alerting pipelines used by SRE and product teams.\n- Runbooks and automated remediation playbooks.\n\nOut of scope (for this phase):\n- Deep model quality evaluation (LLM hallucination metrics) — covered by Optimize/product.\n- Billing/charging changes for customers.\n\nStakeholders and lightweight RACI:\n- Eng-SRE (lead): monitoring, alerting, runbooks, incident postmortem cadence — R\n- Serving Runtime: implementation of instrumentation, fallback hooks, canary flags — A\n- Observability: dashboards, trace sampling, log retention settings — C\n- Platform Engineering: infra capacity policies, autoscaling safety nets — C\n- Product-Hosted-API: product SLO definition & customer-facing comms — I\n- Solutions Eng / Support: pilot adoption and customer escalation play — C\n(Notes: R=Responsible, A=Accountable, C=Consulted, I=Informed)\n\nSignals, tentative metrics and starter targets (provisional — iterate after telemetry baseline):\n- Request Success Rate (5xx + model-load errors): baseline measurement window = 14d; pilot SLO target = 99.7% per 30d for non-burst endpoints.\n- 95th/99th token-latency for inference: capture per-model and per-route; pilot latency SLO = 95th <= 300ms on fast-models, 99th <= 750ms.\n- Model load latency and success (artifact fetch / weight deserialization): target = 99.9% successful within 15s.\n- KV cache hit ratio and tail latency impact: signal only for services opting into KV caching; target: maintain degradation <10% customer impact during cache warmups.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Dependability Compass — cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/dependability-compass-cross-team-playmap.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: eng-sre\n\n750ms.\n- Model load latency and success (artifact fetch / weight deserialization): target = 99.9% successful within 15s.\n- KV cache hit ratio and tail latency impact: signal only for services opting into KV caching; target: maintain degradation <10% customer impact during cache warmups.\n\nMonitoring & alerting pattern:\n- Three alert tiers: WARNING (signal trending bad), INCIDENT (customer-impacting degradation), OUTAGE (SLA violation imminent or occurring).\n- Use metric-derived anomaly windows + heatmap of errors by region/model to reduce noisy pager noise.\n- Attach runbook link in alert payload; require initial triage within 10 minutes for INCIDENT.\n\nRunbooks and automation (practical examples):\n- Runbook: high 5xx rate from a model-serving pod: steps — 1) check model-weight load errors, 2) check OOMs, 3) scale down circuit-breaker, 4) failover to model-variant v2 with pinned weights, 5) engage fallback routing.\n- Automation: when model-load errors > threshold on 3 hosts in 5m, automatically mark model variant as degraded and route new requests to fallback pool. Manual approval required before re-enable.\n\nCanary and rollout pattern (phase gates):\nPhase 0 (instrument + baseline) — 3 weeks\n- Implement key metrics and traces for pilot services. Pair SRE + runtime eng.\n- Build dashboard templates and export baseline numbers.\n\nPhase 1 (soft SLOs + runbooks) — 4 weeks\n- Publish soft SLO targets (non-punitive) and runbooks.\n- Run canaries on internal traffic only.\n\nPhase 2 (automated fallback + guarded SLOs) — 6 weeks\n- Add automated fallback policy for the most common failure (model-load).\n- Start rolling SLOs to small customer cohorts behind a feature flag.\n\nPhase 3 (broader enforcement) — 6–8 weeks\n- Expand enforcement, ensure platform controls prevent noisy autoscale oscillations.\n- Complete postmortem playbooks and SLO reporting.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Dependability Compass — cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/dependability-compass-cross-team-playmap.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: eng-sre\n\nmost common failure (model-load).\n- Start rolling SLOs to small customer cohorts behind a feature flag.\n\nPhase 3 (broader enforcement) — 6–8 weeks\n- Expand enforcement, ensure platform controls prevent noisy autoscale oscillations.\n- Complete postmortem playbooks and SLO reporting.\n\nSprint-by-sprint starter backlog (first 8 sprints, two-week sprints assumed):\nSprint 1: metrics schema, instrumentation hooks merged, dashboard skeletons, export baseline script.\nSprint 2: alert definitions (warning/incident/outage), basic runbook drafts, link to oncall rotation.\nSprint 3: implement canary flag, traffic routing for canary, label propagation for traces.\nSprint 4: automation prototype for model-load fallback, test harness for rollback.\nSprint 5: pilot on Dedicated infra (two services), SRE-led chaos runbook validation.\nSprint 6: telemetry-driven SLO adjustments, comms template for customers.\nSprint 7: scaling safety-net work (platform autoscale playbooks), cost-impact review.\nSprint 8: finalize runbooks, production rollouts for cohort A, dashboarding for exec summary.\n\nCross-team dependency map (key dependencies that block progress):\n- Serving Runtime needs to expose model load/error tags and a per-request model-variant identifier. Blocker: missing tagging per request.\n- Observability needs to add a low-cost trace sampling policy and retention for 30d for pilot metrics. Blocker: retention quota limits in prod logging account.\n- Platform must provide dedicated canary pools and feature-flag gating for traffic split. Blocker: infra quotas for dedicated GPUs.\n\nRisk register & mitigation notes:\n- Risk: Alert fatigue causing ignored incidents. Mitigation: implement signal aggregation and reduce noisy low-value alerts before escalations.\n- Risk: Fallback policies mask underlying reliability problems. Mitigation: ensure fallback triggers incident creation and postmortem requirement.\n- Risk: Costs from additional telemetry and retention. Mitigation: use targeted sampling and short retention for verbose traces; keep metrics high-level.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Dependability Compass — cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/dependability-compass-cross-team-playmap.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: eng-sre\n\naggregation and reduce noisy low-value alerts before escalations.\n- Risk: Fallback policies mask underlying reliability problems. Mitigation: ensure fallback triggers incident creation and postmortem requirement.\n- Risk: Costs from additional telemetry and retention. Mitigation: use targeted sampling and short retention for verbose traces; keep metrics high-level.\n\nCustomer communications and escalations:\n- For pilots: proactive notice to pilot customers outlining expected maintenance windows and rollback behavior.\n- For broader rollouts: staged emails + in-console banner with opt-out for early customers.\n- Support play: Solutions Eng to own first-line customer comms, SRE to own technical explanation and remediation timeline.\n\nOpen questions (to be resolved in the next working sync):\n- Which product routes should be in the initial two pilot services? proposal: text-generation (low-latency path) + embeddings (throughput path).\n- What is acceptable cost delta for adding trace retention for pilot services? target: <10% increase in observability bill for pilot.\n- How do we align model-variant pinning semantics across hosted and private customers? need design doc from Serving Runtime.\n\nNext immediate actions (owners + due dates):\n- Ethan Park: create dashboard templates and baseline export job — due 2026-06-25.\n- Aisha Patel: draft runbook templates and run triage play — due 2026-06-28.\n- Mariano Gomez: (Observability) propose sampling/retention plan — due 2026-06-30.\n- Ravi Kapoor: check infra quotas for canary pools and report blockers — due 2026-07-02.\n\nAppendix: notes for pairing sessions and quick checklists\n- Pairing rule: every change that affects an alert or runbook must have at least one SRE reviewer and one owning-service reviewer.\n- Quick triage checklist for oncall: always record first-action timestamp, whether automatic fallback executed, and whether customer impact (yes/no).",

document.title: Dependability Compass — cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability
document.content:
{
  "title": "Dependability Compass — cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability",
  "owner": "Ethan Park",
  "drive_area": "shared_drives",
  "path": "shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering",
  "doc_type": "doc",
  "created_at": "2026-06-18",
  "last_modified": "2026-07-02",
  "collaborators": [
    "Aisha Patel",
    "Mariana Gomez",
    "Ravi Kapoor",
    "Lina Zhou"
  ],
  "team": "eng-sre",
  "status": "in_review",
  "tags": [
    "dependability",
    "playmap",
    "model-serving",
    "slo",
    "canary",
    "runbook"
  ],
  "linked_artifacts": [
    "CONFLUENCE-REL/Dependability-Compass",
    "JIRA-REL-517",
    "github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/884",
    "slack:#sre-ops"
  ],
  "content": "WORKING DRAFT — Dependability Compass: cross-team playmap for model-serving reliability

Purpose and context:
- This doc captures a concrete cross-functional plan to operationalize reliability goals for model-serving surfaces (hosted API, dedicated, private).
- Focus: translate product-level availability and correctness expectations into measurable signals, ownership, integration tasks, and a pragmatic rollout path that minimizes customer impact while improving long-term observability and remediation speed.
- Audience: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, Observability, Product-Hosted-API, Solutions Eng, Support.

High-level objectives (what success looks like):
1) Observable, actionable signals for the top three failure modes across model-serving (model-load failures, KV cache regressions, tail-latency spikes).
2) Clear ownership and runbooks for each signal with measurable reduction targets in MTTD/MTTR over rolling 90-day windows.
3) A staged SLO adoption pattern that lets teams opt into strict error/latency targets with canary rollouts and automated fallback policies.
4) Two pilot services on dedicated infra with full pipeline (dashboards, alerts, automated rollback) within Q3 2026.

Guiding principles:
- Incremental: instrument first, then set targets, then automate responses.
- Customer-impact focused: prioritize signals that map to user-visible degradation.
- Low blast radius: use progressive rollout (canary, cohort) for any enforcement.
- Cross-team pairing: each milestone requires an SRE + owning-engineer co-shipper.

Scope (in):
- Model-serving control plane and inference runtime path (request ingress, KV cache, model weights load, token generation latency).
- Observability (metrics, traces, logs) and alerting pipelines used by SRE and product teams.
- Runbooks and automated remediation playbooks.

Out of scope (for this phase):
- Deep model quality evaluation (LLM hallucination metrics) — covered by Optimize/product.
- Billing/charging changes for customers.

Stakeholders and lightweight RACI:
- Eng-SRE (lead): monitoring, alerting, runbooks, incident postmortem cadence — R
- Serving Runtime: implementation of instrumentation, fallback hooks, canary flags — A
- Observability: dashboards, trace sampling, log retention settings — C
- Platform Engineering: infra capacity policies, autoscaling safety nets — C
- Product-Hosted-API: product SLO definition & customer-facing comms — I
- Solutions Eng / Support: pilot adoption and customer escalation play — C
(Notes: R=Responsible, A=Accountable, C=Consulted, I=Informed)

Signals, tentative metrics and starter targets (provisional — iterate after telemetry baseline):
- Request Success Rate (5xx + model-load errors): baseline measurement window = 14d; pilot SLO target = 99.7% per 30d for non-burst endpoints.
- 95th/99th token-latency for inference: capture per-model and per-route; pilot latency SLO = 95th <= 300ms on fast-models, 99th <= 750ms.
- Model load latency and success (artifact fetch / weight deserialization): target = 99.9% successful within 15s.
- KV cache hit ratio and tail latency impact: signal only for services opting into KV caching; target: maintain degradation <10% customer impact during cache warmups.

Monitoring & alerting pattern:
- Three alert tiers: WARNING (signal trending bad), INCIDENT (customer-impacting degradation), OUTAGE (SLA violation imminent or occurring).
- Use metric-derived anomaly windows + heatmap of errors by region/model to reduce noisy pager noise.
- Attach runbook link in alert payload; require initial triage within 10 minutes for INCIDENT.

Runbooks and automation (practical examples):
- Runbook: high 5xx rate from a model-serving pod: steps — 1) check model-weight load errors, 2) check OOMs, 3) scale down circuit-breaker, 4) failover to model-variant v2 with pinned weights, 5) engage fallback routing.
- Automation: when model-load errors > threshold on 3 hosts in 5m, automatically mark model variant as degraded and route new requests to fallback pool. Manual approval required before re-enable.

Canary and rollout pattern (phase gates):
Phase 0 (instrument + baseline) — 3 weeks
- Implement key metrics and traces for pilot services. Pair SRE + runtime eng.
- Build dashboard templates and export baseline numbers.

Phase 1 (soft SLOs + runbooks) — 4 weeks
- Publish soft SLO targets (non-punitive) and runbooks.
- Run canaries on internal traffic only.

Phase 2 (automated fallback + guarded SLOs) — 6 weeks
- Add automated fallback policy for the most common failure (model-load).
- Start rolling SLOs to small customer cohorts behind a feature flag.

Phase 3 (broader enforcement) — 6–8 weeks
- Expand enforcement, ensure platform controls prevent noisy autoscale oscillations.
- Complete postmortem playbooks and SLO reporting.

Sprint-by-sprint starter backlog (first 8 sprints, two-week sprints assumed):
Sprint 1: metrics schema, instrumentation hooks merged, dashboard skeletons, export baseline script.
Sprint 2: alert definitions (warning/incident/outage), basic runbook drafts, link to oncall rotation.
Sprint 3: implement canary flag, traffic routing for canary, label propagation for traces.
Sprint 4: automation prototype for model-load fallback, test harness for rollback.
Sprint 5: pilot on Dedicated infra (two services), SRE-led chaos runbook validation.
Sprint 6: telemetry-driven SLO adjustments, comms template for customers.
Sprint 7: scaling safety-net work (platform autoscale playbooks), cost-impact review.
Sprint 8: finalize runbooks, production rollouts for cohort A, dashboarding for exec summary.

Cross-team dependency map (key dependencies that block progress):
- Serving Runtime needs to expose model load/error tags and a per-request model-variant identifier. Blocker: missing tagging per request.
- Observability needs to add a low-cost trace sampling policy and retention for 30d for pilot metrics. Blocker: retention quota limits in prod logging account.
- Platform must provide dedicated canary pools and feature-flag gating for traffic split. Blocker: infra quotas for dedicated GPUs.

Risk register & mitigation notes:
- Risk: Alert fatigue causing ignored incidents. Mitigation: implement signal aggregation and reduce noisy low-value alerts before escalations.
- Risk: Fallback policies mask underlying reliability problems. Mitigation: ensure fallback triggers incident creation and postmortem requirement.
- Risk: Costs from additional telemetry and retention. Mitigation: use targeted sampling and short retention for verbose traces; keep metrics high-level.

Customer communications and escalations:
- For pilots: proactive notice to pilot customers outlining expected maintenance windows and rollback behavior.
- For broader rollouts: staged emails + in-console banner with opt-out for early customers.
- Support play: Solutions Eng to own first-line customer comms, SRE to own technical explanation and remediation timeline.

Open questions (to be resolved in the next working sync):
- Which product routes should be in the initial two pilot services? proposal: text-generation (low-latency path) + embeddings (throughput path).
- What is acceptable cost delta for adding trace retention for pilot services? target: <10% increase in observability bill for pilot.
- How do we align model-variant pinning semantics across hosted and private customers? need design doc from Serving Runtime.

- Ethan Park: create dashboard templates and baseline export job — due 2026-06-25.
- Aisha Patel: draft runbook templates and run triage play — due 2026-06-28.
- Mariano Gomez: (Observability) propose sampling/retention plan — due 2026-06-30.
- Ravi Kapoor: check infra quotas for canary pools and report blockers — due 2026-07-02.

Appendix: notes for pairing sessions and quick checklists
- Pairing rule: every change that affects an alert or runbook must have at least one SRE reviewer and one owning-service reviewer.
- Quick triage checklist for oncall: always record first-action timestamp, whether automatic fallback executed, and whether customer impact (yes/no).

- This is intentionally prescriptive at the tactical level to get cross-team alignment quickly. Expect adjustments to SLO targets after we ingest baseline telemetry.
- Please comment on the proposed pilot services and add any missing failure modes you’ve observed in the past 6 months.

End of document.

{

    "id": "dsid_88d9d5d9a1b746e6ad01cba7bf0da5c4",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure.json",
    "title": "GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{
  "title": "GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)",
  "space": "eng-infra",
  "author": "Irene Choi",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-06",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-12",
  "reviewers": [
    "Rafael Mendes",
    "Miles Thornton",
    "Vanessa Ortiz",
    "Victor Alvarez",
    "Mina Haddad",
    "Peter Holtz"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "runbook",
    "gpu-pools",
    "failover",
    "regional-impairment",
    "dedicated",
    "hosted-api",
    "capacity",
    "sre"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://eng-sre/runbooks/hosted-api-regional-failover-runbook",
    "confluence://eng-platform/runbooks/routing-policy-failover-controller-runbook",
    "confluence://eng-platform/systems-and-services/region-health-service",
    "confluence://eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/cross-region-dns-and-anycast-routing-notes",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-042-failover-trigger-signal-hierarchy",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-043-automated-routing-policy-rollback",
    "confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/failover-signal-dashboards-spec"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "content": "## Purpose\nThis runbook describes how to safely **drain** and, if needed, **evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:\n- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)\n- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated\n- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)\n\n**Drain** means: stop placing new work on a pool and let in-flight work complete (or age out) while routing shifts traffic elsewhere.\n\n**Evacuation** means: drain + expedite termination/migration of remaining workloads (with stricter safeguards), typically when the region is actively failing.\n\nThis procedure must be coordinated with routing (policy engine + failover controller) to avoid creating a thundering herd, retry storms, or overload in the target region.\n\n---\n\n## Scope / ownership\n**Applies to:**\n- Hosted API serving GPU pools (multi-tenant)\n- Dedicated customer pools (tenant-isolated)\n\n**Not covered:**\n- Customer-managed on-prem clusters (see Private deployment guidance)\n\n**Primary on-call:** Infra (Fleet/Capacity) + SRE\n\n**Key coordination roles:**\n- SRE on-call (incident commander / traffic shift approvals)\n- Routing/control plane on-call (policy flips, hold-down/rollback)\n- Network on-call (reachability validation)\n- Dedicated support liaison (customer notifications when required)\n\n---\n\n## When to use this runbook\nUse this runbook when **any** of the following is true:\n1) Failover controller recommends or executes regional failover and indicates **pool drain required**.\n2) Region health is **UNHEALTHY** (reachability authoritative) and continuing to accept new requests will increase customer impact.\n3) GPU pool shows sustained symptoms consistent with regional impairment:\n   - Elevated 5xx burn rate + corroborated reachability failures\n   - Severe tail latency burn with network symptoms\n   - Control plane errors impacting scheduling/placement\n4) Planned controlled failover test (game day) includes pool drain/evacuation steps.\n\n---\n\n## Safety principles (read before acting)\n1) **Traffic shift first, then drain.** Do not drain capacity that is still receiving significant new traffic.\n2) **Prefer drain over evac.** Evacuation is higher risk; use only when the region is actively impairing service or the pool is unstable.\n3) **Do not flap.** Respect automation hold-down timers and rate limits. Multiple flip/drain cycles worsen customer impact.\n4) **Dedicated requires explicit tenant guardrails.** Dedicated pools should not be drained without verifying:\n   - Target region capacity reservation/headroom\n   - Data residency / contractual constraints\n   - Customer comms requirements (if any)\n5) **Always keep at least one healthy route.** Ensure routing fallback exists before reducing serving capacity.\n\n---\n\n## Prerequisites / access\nYou must have:\n- Access to internal tooling (CLI + dashboards)\n- Ability to read routing policy state and region health\n- Permission to initiate pool drain (role: infra-oncall or delegated)\n\n**Tools referenced in this runbook:**\n- `failoverctl` (failover controller/operator CLI)\n- `poolctl` (fleet pool management CLI)\n- Observability dashboards (failover signals, pool saturation, drain progress)\n\nIf you do not have access, page **Infra On-Call** and **SRE On-Call**.\n\n---\n\n## Inputs to collect (5\u201310 minutes)\nCapture these before changing anything (paste into incident timeline):\n\n### A) Determine event type\n- [ ] **Planned** (game day / scheduled test)\n- [ ] **Unplanned** (real impairment)\n\n### B) Identify affected surface area\n- [ ] Hosted API routes/models affected (e.g., chat, embeddings)\n- [ ] Dedicated tenants affected (list tenant IDs + tiers)\n- [ ] Region(s): source region to drain, target region(s)\n\n### C) Confirm routing state (must-have)\nFrom routing team or `failoverctl`:\n- Current policy state: is the region already de-preferred / disabled?\n- Controller mode: dry-run vs execute; approval required?\n- Any hold-down timers active?\n\n### D) Confirm region health signals (corroboration)\n- Reachability probes (authoritative)\n- 5xx burn + tail latency burn\n- Capacity headroom in target region(s)\n- Network status / provider status page notes\n\n---\n\n## Decision matrix: Drain vs Evacuate\n**Default:** Drain.\n\nProceed with **Drain** if:\n- Routing has shifted or is shifting traffic away\n- Region is degraded but not fully unreachable\n- Control plane is stable enough to manage pool state\n\nProceed with **Evacuation** if **any** of the following:\n- Region becomes unreachable or intermittently unreachable\n- Control plane is failing (cannot reliably schedule/monitor)\n- Pool health is collapsing (crash loops, node loss, scheduler failures)\n- Continuing to wait for natural drain is increasing customer impact\n\nIf unsure, choose **Drain** and re-evaluate after 10 minutes.\n\n---\n\n## Procedure 1: Coordinated drain (recommended)\n### Step 1 \u2014 Establish coordination + announce intent\n- [ ] Confirm incident channel and owner(s): SRE IC + Infra lead\n- [ ] Post in incident channel:\n  - Region + pool names\n  - Drain intent\n  - Target region(s)\n  - Expected customer impact (ideally none beyond transient retries)\n\n### Step 2 \u2014 Ensure routing is shifting away (gate)\n**Gate: do not drain until routing is in motion.**\n\nVerify one of:\n- Failover controller has executed policy flip away from the region, OR\n- Routing on-call confirms manual policy update completed, OR\n- For a controlled test: the scheduled routing step is complete\n\nSuggested checks:\n- `failoverctl status --region us-east` (example)\n- Dashboard: Failover Signals \u2192 Policy flips + traffic distribution\n\nExpected state before draining:\n- Traffic share in source region trending down\n- Target region request rate increasing but within safe headroom\n\n### Step 3 \u2014 Verify target region headroom (gate)\n**Gate: ensure target can absorb traffic without overload.**\n\nCheck:\n- GPU utilization and queue depth\n- Token latency (p95/p99) and 5xx in target region\n- Admission control / circuit breaker status\n\nIf target region is near saturation:\n- Coordinate with routing to split traffic across multiple regions\n- Enable load shedding / stricter retries before draining further\n\n### Step 4 \u2014 Initiate drain on the pool\nUse pool tooling to stop new placements while allowing in-flight work to complete.\n\nExample:\n- `poolctl drain start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason \"regional_failover\" --ttl 60m`\n\nRecommended drain settings:\n- **Placement disabled:** on\n- **Grace period:** 15\u201330 minutes for Hosted API pools; 30\u201360 minutes for Dedicated pools (unless evac is required)\n- **TTL:** set to prevent \u201cforgotten drain\u201d (default 60 minutes)\n\nFor Dedicated pools, prefer per-tenant drain:\n- `poolctl drain start --pool <DEDICATED_POOL_ID> --tenant <TENANT_ID> --ttl 60m`\n\n### Step 5 \u2014 Monitor drain progress\nWatch until drain completes or stabilizes.\n\nMonitor:\n- Active sessions / in-flight requests\n- KV cache eviction progress (if available)\n- Node health and autoscaler behavior\n- Drain progress metric (Dedicated): `dedicated_drain_progress{pool=...}`\n\nSuggested cadence:\n- 2\u20133 minute updates in incident channel\n\n### Step 6 \u2014 Validate outcomes\nDrain is \u201csuccessful\u201d when:\n- New placements are near zero in the drained pool\n- In-flight work trends toward zero without sharp 5xx spikes\n- Target region latency/5xx stays within acceptable bounds\n\nIf drain causes elevated errors:\n- Check gateway retry budgets and circuit breaker status\n- Confirm client redirect handling (streaming reconnect)\n- Slow down the drain (increase grace / pause) before proceeding\n\n### Step 7 \u2014 Lock state and handoff\nOnce drained:\n- Mark pool as drained with a clear tag/annotation\n- Ensure routing policy remains stable (respect hold-down)\n- Decide whether to keep drained (standby) or proceed to evacuation/scale-down\n\n---\n\n## Procedure 2: Evacuation (higher risk; use when required)\n### Step 1 \u2014 Confirm evacuation authorization\nEvacuation should be approved by:\n- SRE IC (or SRE on-call) AND\n- Infra on-call lead\n\nIf Dedicated customers are impacted, loop in Support liaison (Dev Patel / Owen Phillips) for comms coordination.\n\n### Step 2 \u2014 Freeze routing changes (avoid oscillation)\nBefore aggressive actions, confirm:\n- Routing policy is stable and will not automatically revert during evacuation.\n- Automation rate limits/anti-flap timers are understood.\n\nIf rollback is likely, pause and coordinate with routing.\n\n### Step 3 \u2014 Force stop placements and accelerate shutdown\nExample:\n- `poolctl evacuate start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason \"region_unreachable\" --max-parallel 20 --force-after 10m`\n\nGuidance:\n- Limit parallelism to avoid mass reconnect storms.\n- For multi-tenant Hosted API pools, prioritize stability over speed.\n\n### Step 4 \u2014 Protect target region from overload\nDuring evacuation, expect:\n- Retry spikes\n- Connection churn\n- Increased cold starts and cache misses\n\nMitigations (coordinate with gateway/routing owners):\n- Enforce `Retry-After` overload responses\n- Temporarily tighten gateway retry budgets\n- Increase admission control strictness to maintain tail latency SLOs\n\n### Step 5 \u2014 Validate and complete evacuation\nSuccess criteria:\n- Pool has no schedulable capacity\n- All nodes are cordoned/removed or otherwise inactive\n- Traffic is steady in target region(s)\n\nIf control plane is failing and you cannot complete evacuation cleanly:\n- Escalate to Control Plane on-call\n- Capture evidence and stop making repeated changes\n\n---\n\n## Rollback / abort criteria\nStop and reassess if any of the following occurs:\n- Target region enters sustained overload (rapid 5xx increase, severe tail latency burn)\n- Routing policy begins oscillating (auto rollback triggers) during drain/evac\n- Drain tool reports inconsistent state (stuck drain, missing signals)\n- Dedicated tenant violates residency/region constraints (security/compliance risk)\n\nRollback options (coordinate with routing):\n1) Pause drain/evac:\n   - `poolctl drain pause --pool <POOL_ID>`\n2) Re-enable placements temporarily (only if routing is still sending traffic):\n   - `poolctl drain stop --pool <POOL_ID> --reason \"rollback\"`\n3) Slow traffic shift (policy engine changes) rather than reverting fully\n\nAlways record who approved rollback and why.\n\n---\n\n## Communication checklist\n### Internal\n- [ ] Incident channel updates every 5\u201310 minutes during active drain/evac\n- [ ] Incident-bot timeline annotations (verify failover/drain markers are present)\n- [ ] Link dashboards used for decisions\n\n### Customer-facing (when applicable)\nHosted API:\n- Status page updates are handled by SRE IC per comms playbook.\n\nDedicated:\n- If draining a Dedicated pool that can impact throughput/latency, coordinate with Support/CS for proactive notice per account requirements.\n\nReference: Regional Failover Communication Playbook.\n\n---\n\n## Post-action validation (required)\nAfter drain/evac is complete:\n- [ ] Confirm policy state + traffic distribution is stable for at least 30 minutes\n- [ ] Confirm no sustained error budget burn in target region\n- [ ] Confirm Dedicated drain progress metrics are clean and saved\n- [ ] Ensure pools are either:\n  - left drained intentionally with TTL + owner, OR\n  - returned to service with an explicit plan\n\nCreate follow-up tasks if:\n- Drain took longer than expected\n- Any transient customer impact occurred (even if within SLO)\n- Any manual steps were unclear or tools were missing\n\n---\n\n## Notes on Dedicated vs Hosted\n### Dedicated pools\n- Drain per tenant/pool; do not batch multiple tenants without explicit approval.\n- Verify contract constraints (region pinning) before shifting.\n- Prefer \u201cwarm standby\u201d capacity in target region if available.\n\n### Hosted API pools\n- High concurrency + streaming means connection churn is a primary risk.\n- Expect higher cache miss rates after traffic shift; watch tail latency.\n\n---\n\n## Metrics / dashboards to use\nDuring drain/evac, monitor:\n- Region traffic split by route/model\n- 5xx burn rate and tail latency burn (source + target)\n- Reachability probe status (authoritative)\n- GPU utilization, queue depth, and admission control rejections\n- Drain progress metrics for Dedicated\n\nDashboards:\n- Failover Signals Dashboard (reachability, burn rates, policy flips)\n- Fleet Capacity Dashboard (headroom per region/pool)\n- Dedicated Drain Progress Dashboard (per tenant/pool)\n\n---\n\n## Appendix A \u2014 Example incident timeline snippet\nCopy/paste template:\n- T+00: Confirmed reachability failures in us-east (probe fail 80%); 5xx burn corroborated.\n- T+03: Routing policy flipped us-east weight 100%\u21920% (failoverctl execution id: \u2026).\n- T+06: Verified eu-west headroom (GPU util 62%, queue stable).\n- T+08: Initiated pool drain on us-east pool rw-hosted-ue1-a (ttl 60m).\n- T+18: Drain progress 70%; no sustained 5xx spikes; target p99 stable.\n- T+26: Drain complete; placements disabled; in-flight near zero.\n\n---\n\n## Appendix B \u2014 Common failure modes and fixes\n1) **Drain appears stuck**\n   - Cause: long-lived streaming sessions or stuck workers\n   - Action: extend grace period; for evac, set conservative force-after; coordinate with gateway to reduce retries\n\n2) **Target region overload after drain start**\n   - Cause: traffic shift too fast + cache miss + retry storm\n   - Action: pause drain; split traffic across multiple regions; enable stricter admission control; tune retries\n\n3) **Oscillation (routing flips back and forth)**\n   - Cause: noisy signals, hold-down mis-tuned\n   - Action: stop making capacity changes; coordinate with routing to stabilize; follow ADR-043 rollback guardrails\n\n4) **Dedicated tenant capacity shortfall**\n   - Cause: reservations/headroom insufficient in target region\n   - Action: halt drain; allocate burst capacity if available; coordinate with Dedicated product + Support for comms\n\n---\n\n## Change log\n- 2026-02-12: Added evacuation guardrails, Dedicated per-tenant guidance, and explicit routing gates; aligned terminology with failover controller audit events.\n- 2026-01-20: Initial publication for Q1 game day support.\n",

Content: ## Purpose
This runbook describes how to safely **drain** and, if needed, **evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:
- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)
- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated
- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)",

      "text": "[Document context]
Title: GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: eng-infra

evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:
- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)
- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated
- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)

**Drain** means: stop placing new work on a pool and let in-flight work complete (or age out) while routing shifts traffic elsewhere.

**Evacuation** means: drain + expedite termination/migration of remaining workloads (with stricter safeguards), typically when the region is actively failing.

This procedure must be coordinated with routing (policy engine + failover controller) to avoid creating a thundering herd, retry storms, or overload in the target region.

---

## Scope / ownership
**Applies to:**
- Hosted API serving GPU pools (multi-tenant)
- Dedicated customer pools (tenant-isolated)

**Not covered:**
- Customer-managed on-prem clusters (see Private deployment guidance)

**Primary on-call:** Infra (Fleet/Capacity) + SRE

**Key coordination roles:**
- SRE on-call (incident commander / traffic shift approvals)
- Routing/control plane on-call (policy flips, hold-down/rollback)
- Network on-call (reachability validation)
- Dedicated support liaison (customer notifications when required)

---

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when **any** of the following is true:
1) Failover controller recommends or executes regional failover and indicates **pool drain required**.
2) Region health is **UNHEALTHY** (reachability authoritative) and continuing to accept new requests will increase customer impact.
3) GPU pool shows sustained symptoms consistent with regional impairment:
   - Elevated 5xx burn rate + corroborated reachability failures
   - Severe tail latency burn with network symptoms
   - Control plane errors impacting scheduling/placement
4) Planned controlled failover test (game day) includes pool drain/evacuation steps.

Title: GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: eng-infra

symptoms consistent with regional impairment:
   - Elevated 5xx burn rate + corroborated reachability failures
   - Severe tail latency burn with network symptoms
   - Control plane errors impacting scheduling/placement
4) Planned controlled failover test (game day) includes pool drain/evacuation steps.

---

## Safety principles (read before acting)
1) **Traffic shift first, then drain.** Do not drain capacity that is still receiving significant new traffic.
2) **Prefer drain over evac.** Evacuation is higher risk; use only when the region is actively impairing service or the pool is unstable.
3) **Do not flap.** Respect automation hold-down timers and rate limits. Multiple flip/drain cycles worsen customer impact.
4) **Dedicated requires explicit tenant guardrails.** Dedicated pools should not be drained without verifying:
   - Target region capacity reservation/headroom
   - Data residency / contractual constraints
   - Customer comms requirements (if any)
5) **Always keep at least one healthy route.** Ensure routing fallback exists before reducing serving capacity.

---

## Prerequisites / access
You must have:
- Access to internal tooling (CLI + dashboards)
- Ability to read routing policy state and region health
- Permission to initiate pool drain (role: infra-oncall or delegated)

**Tools referenced in this runbook:**
- `failoverctl` (failover controller/operator CLI)
- `poolctl` (fleet pool management CLI)
- Observability dashboards (failover signals, pool saturation, drain progress)

If you do not have access, page **Infra On-Call** and **SRE On-Call**.

---

## Inputs to collect (5–10 minutes)
Capture these before changing anything (paste into incident timeline):

### A) Determine event type

- [ ] **Unplanned** (real impairment)",

---

## Inputs to collect (5–10 minutes)
Capture these before changing anything (paste into incident timeline):

### A) Determine event type
- [ ] **Planned** (game day / scheduled test)
- [ ] **Unplanned** (real impairment)

### B) Identify affected surface area
- [ ] Hosted API routes/models affected (e.g., chat, embeddings)
- [ ] Dedicated tenants affected (list tenant IDs + tiers)
- [ ] Region(s): source region to drain, target region(s)

### C) Confirm routing state (must-have)
From routing team or `failoverctl`:
- Current policy state: is the region already de-preferred / disabled?
- Controller mode: dry-run vs execute; approval required?
- Any hold-down timers active?

### D) Confirm region health signals (corroboration)
- Reachability probes (authoritative)
- 5xx burn + tail latency burn
- Capacity headroom in target region(s)
- Network status / provider status page notes

---

## Decision matrix: Drain vs Evacuate
**Default:** Drain.

Proceed with **Drain** if:
- Routing has shifted or is shifting traffic away
- Region is degraded but not fully unreachable
- Control plane is stable enough to manage pool state

Proceed with **Evacuation** if **any** of the following:
- Region becomes unreachable or intermittently unreachable
- Control plane is failing (cannot reliably schedule/monitor)
- Pool health is collapsing (crash loops, node loss, scheduler failures)
- Continuing to wait for natural drain is increasing customer impact

If unsure, choose **Drain** and re-evaluate after 10 minutes.

---

## Procedure 1: Coordinated drain (recommended)
### Step 1 — Establish coordination + announce intent
- [ ] Confirm incident channel and owner(s): SRE IC + Infra lead
- [ ] Post in incident channel:
  - Region + pool names
  - Drain intent
  - Target region(s)
  - Expected customer impact (ideally none beyond transient retries)",

Title: GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: eng-infra

— Establish coordination + announce intent
- [ ] Confirm incident channel and owner(s): SRE IC + Infra lead
- [ ] Post in incident channel:
  - Region + pool names
  - Drain intent
  - Target region(s)
  - Expected customer impact (ideally none beyond transient retries)

### Step 2 — Ensure routing is shifting away (gate)
**Gate: do not drain until routing is in motion.**

Verify one of:
- Failover controller has executed policy flip away from the region, OR
- Routing on-call confirms manual policy update completed, OR
- For a controlled test: the scheduled routing step is complete

Suggested checks:
- `failoverctl status --region us-east` (example)
- Dashboard: Failover Signals → Policy flips + traffic distribution

Expected state before draining:
- Traffic share in source region trending down
- Target region request rate increasing but within safe headroom

### Step 3 — Verify target region headroom (gate)
**Gate: ensure target can absorb traffic without overload.**

Check:
- GPU utilization and queue depth
- Token latency (p95/p99) and 5xx in target region
- Admission control / circuit breaker status

If target region is near saturation:
- Coordinate with routing to split traffic across multiple regions
- Enable load shedding / stricter retries before draining further

### Step 4 — Initiate drain on the pool
Use pool tooling to stop new placements while allowing in-flight work to complete.

Example:
- `poolctl drain start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "regional_failover" --ttl 60m`

Recommended drain settings:
- **Placement disabled:** on
- **Grace period:** 15–30 minutes for Hosted API pools; 30–60 minutes for Dedicated pools (unless evac is required)
- **TTL:** set to prevent “forgotten drain” (default 60 minutes)

For Dedicated pools, prefer per-tenant drain:
- `poolctl drain start --pool <DEDICATED_POOL_ID> --tenant <TENANT_ID> --ttl 60m`",

unless evac is required)
- **TTL:** set to prevent “forgotten drain” (default 60 minutes)

For Dedicated pools, prefer per-tenant drain:
- `poolctl drain start --pool <DEDICATED_POOL_ID> --tenant <TENANT_ID> --ttl 60m`

### Step 5 — Monitor drain progress
Watch until drain completes or stabilizes.

Monitor:
- Active sessions / in-flight requests
- KV cache eviction progress (if available)
- Node health and autoscaler behavior
- Drain progress metric (Dedicated): `dedicated_drain_progress{pool=...}`

Suggested cadence:
- 2–3 minute updates in incident channel

### Step 6 — Validate outcomes
Drain is “successful” when:
- New placements are near zero in the drained pool
- In-flight work trends toward zero without sharp 5xx spikes
- Target region latency/5xx stays within acceptable bounds

If drain causes elevated errors:
- Check gateway retry budgets and circuit breaker status
- Confirm client redirect handling (streaming reconnect)
- Slow down the drain (increase grace / pause) before proceeding

### Step 7 — Lock state and handoff
Once drained:
- Mark pool as drained with a clear tag/annotation
- Ensure routing policy remains stable (respect hold-down)
- Decide whether to keep drained (standby) or proceed to evacuation/scale-down

---

## Procedure 2: Evacuation (higher risk; use when required)
### Step 1 — Confirm evacuation authorization
Evacuation should be approved by:
- SRE IC (or SRE on-call) AND
- Infra on-call lead

If Dedicated customers are impacted, loop in Support liaison (Dev Patel / Owen Phillips) for comms coordination.

### Step 2 — Freeze routing changes (avoid oscillation)
Before aggressive actions, confirm:
- Routing policy is stable and will not automatically revert during evacuation.
- Automation rate limits/anti-flap timers are understood.

### Step 2 — Freeze routing changes (avoid oscillation)
Before aggressive actions, confirm:
- Routing policy is stable and will not automatically revert during evacuation.
- Automation rate limits/anti-flap timers are understood.

If rollback is likely, pause and coordinate with routing.

### Step 3 — Force stop placements and accelerate shutdown
Example:
- `poolctl evacuate start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "region_unreachable" --max-parallel 20 --force-after 10m`

Guidance:
- Limit parallelism to avoid mass reconnect storms.
- For multi-tenant Hosted API pools, prioritize stability over speed.

### Step 4 — Protect target region from overload
During evacuation, expect:
- Retry spikes
- Connection churn
- Increased cold starts and cache misses

Mitigations (coordinate with gateway/routing owners):
- Enforce `Retry-After` overload responses
- Temporarily tighten gateway retry budgets
- Increase admission control strictness to maintain tail latency SLOs

### Step 5 — Validate and complete evacuation
Success criteria:
- Pool has no schedulable capacity
- All nodes are cordoned/removed or otherwise inactive
- Traffic is steady in target region(s)

If control plane is failing and you cannot complete evacuation cleanly:
- Escalate to Control Plane on-call
- Capture evidence and stop making repeated changes

---

## Rollback / abort criteria
Stop and reassess if any of the following occurs:
- Target region enters sustained overload (rapid 5xx increase, severe tail latency burn)
- Routing policy begins oscillating (auto rollback triggers) during drain/evac
- Drain tool reports inconsistent state (stuck drain, missing signals)
- Dedicated tenant violates residency/region constraints (security/compliance risk)",

      "text": "[Document context]
Title: GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: eng-infra

:
- Target region enters sustained overload (rapid 5xx increase, severe tail latency burn)
- Routing policy begins oscillating (auto rollback triggers) during drain/evac
- Drain tool reports inconsistent state (stuck drain, missing signals)
- Dedicated tenant violates residency/region constraints (security/compliance risk)

Rollback options (coordinate with routing):
1) Pause drain/evac:
   - `poolctl drain pause --pool <POOL_ID>`
2) Re-enable placements temporarily (only if routing is still sending traffic):
   - `poolctl drain stop --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "rollback"`
3) Slow traffic shift (policy engine changes) rather than reverting fully

Always record who approved rollback and why.

---

## Communication checklist
### Internal
- [ ] Incident channel updates every 5–10 minutes during active drain/evac
- [ ] Incident-bot timeline annotations (verify failover/drain markers are present)
- [ ] Link dashboards used for decisions

### Customer-facing (when applicable)
Hosted API:
- Status page updates are handled by SRE IC per comms playbook.

Dedicated:
- If draining a Dedicated pool that can impact throughput/latency, coordinate with Support/CS for proactive notice per account requirements.

Reference: Regional Failover Communication Playbook.

---

## Post-action validation (required)
After drain/evac is complete:
- [ ] Confirm policy state + traffic distribution is stable for at least 30 minutes
- [ ] Confirm no sustained error budget burn in target region
- [ ] Confirm Dedicated drain progress metrics are clean and saved
- [ ] Ensure pools are either:
  - left drained intentionally with TTL + owner, OR
  - returned to service with an explicit plan

Create follow-up tasks if:
- Drain took longer than expected
- Any transient customer impact occurred (even if within SLO)
- Any manual steps were unclear or tools were missing

Title: GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: eng-infra

pools are either:
  - left drained intentionally with TTL + owner, OR
  - returned to service with an explicit plan

Create follow-up tasks if:
- Drain took longer than expected
- Any transient customer impact occurred (even if within SLO)
- Any manual steps were unclear or tools were missing

---

## Notes on Dedicated vs Hosted
### Dedicated pools
- Drain per tenant/pool; do not batch multiple tenants without explicit approval.
- Verify contract constraints (region pinning) before shifting.
- Prefer “warm standby” capacity in target region if available.

### Hosted API pools
- High concurrency + streaming means connection churn is a primary risk.
- Expect higher cache miss rates after traffic shift; watch tail latency.

---

## Metrics / dashboards to use
During drain/evac, monitor:
- Region traffic split by route/model
- 5xx burn rate and tail latency burn (source + target)
- Reachability probe status (authoritative)
- GPU utilization, queue depth, and admission control rejections
- Drain progress metrics for Dedicated

Dashboards:
- Failover Signals Dashboard (reachability, burn rates, policy flips)
- Fleet Capacity Dashboard (headroom per region/pool)
- Dedicated Drain Progress Dashboard (per tenant/pool)

---

## Appendix A — Example incident timeline snippet
Copy/paste template:
- T+00: Confirmed reachability failures in us-east (probe fail 80%); 5xx burn corroborated.
- T+03: Routing policy flipped us-east weight 100%→0% (failoverctl execution id: …).
- T+06: Verified eu-west headroom (GPU util 62%, queue stable).
- T+08: Initiated pool drain on us-east pool rw-hosted-ue1-a (ttl 60m).
- T+18: Drain progress 70%; no sustained 5xx spikes; target p99 stable.
- T+26: Drain complete; placements disabled; in-flight near zero.

+08: Initiated pool drain on us-east pool rw-hosted-ue1-a (ttl 60m).
- T+18: Drain progress 70%; no sustained 5xx spikes; target p99 stable.
- T+26: Drain complete; placements disabled; in-flight near zero.

---

## Appendix B — Common failure modes and fixes
1) **Drain appears stuck**
   - Cause: long-lived streaming sessions or stuck workers
   - Action: extend grace period; for evac, set conservative force-after; coordinate with gateway to reduce retries

2) **Target region overload after drain start**
   - Cause: traffic shift too fast + cache miss + retry storm
   - Action: pause drain; split traffic across multiple regions; enable stricter admission control; tune retries

3) **Oscillation (routing flips back and forth)**
   - Cause: noisy signals, hold-down mis-tuned
   - Action: stop making capacity changes; coordinate with routing to stabilize; follow ADR-043 rollback guardrails

4) **Dedicated tenant capacity shortfall**
   - Cause: reservations/headroom insufficient in target region
   - Action: halt drain; allocate burst capacity if available; coordinate with Dedicated product + Support for comms

- 2026-02-12: Added evacuation guardrails, Dedicated per-tenant guidance, and explicit routing gates; aligned terminology with failover controller audit events.

document.content:
{
  "title": "GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)",
  "space": "eng-infra",
  "author": "Irene Choi",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-06",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-12",
  "reviewers": [
    "Rafael Mendes",
    "Miles Thornton",
    "Vanessa Ortiz",
    "Victor Alvarez",
    "Mina Haddad",
    "Peter Holtz"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "runbook",
    "gpu-pools",
    "failover",
    "regional-impairment",
    "dedicated",
    "hosted-api",
    "capacity",
    "sre"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://eng-sre/runbooks/hosted-api-regional-failover-runbook",
    "confluence://eng-platform/runbooks/routing-policy-failover-controller-runbook",
    "confluence://eng-platform/systems-and-services/region-health-service",
    "confluence://eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/cross-region-dns-and-anycast-routing-notes",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-042-failover-trigger-signal-hierarchy",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-043-automated-routing-policy-rollback",
    "confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/failover-signal-dashboards-spec"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "content": "## Purpose
This runbook describes how to safely **drain** and, if needed, **evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:
- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)
- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated
- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)

**Drain** means: stop placing new work on a pool and let in-flight work complete (or age out) while routing shifts traffic elsewhere.

**Evacuation** means: drain + expedite termination/migration of remaining workloads (with stricter safeguards), typically when the region is actively failing.

This procedure must be coordinated with routing (policy engine + failover controller) to avoid creating a thundering herd, retry storms, or overload in the target region.

---

## Scope / ownership
**Applies to:**
- Hosted API serving GPU pools (multi-tenant)
- Dedicated customer pools (tenant-isolated)

**Not covered:**
- Customer-managed on-prem clusters (see Private deployment guidance)

**Primary on-call:** Infra (Fleet/Capacity) + SRE

**Key coordination roles:**
- SRE on-call (incident commander / traffic shift approvals)
- Routing/control plane on-call (policy flips, hold-down/rollback)
- Network on-call (reachability validation)
- Dedicated support liaison (customer notifications when required)

---

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when **any** of the following is true:
1) Failover controller recommends or executes regional failover and indicates **pool drain required**.
2) Region health is **UNHEALTHY** (reachability authoritative) and continuing to accept new requests will increase customer impact.
3) GPU pool shows sustained symptoms consistent with regional impairment:
   - Elevated 5xx burn rate + corroborated reachability failures
   - Severe tail latency burn with network symptoms
   - Control plane errors impacting scheduling/placement
4) Planned controlled failover test (game day) includes pool drain/evacuation steps.

---

## Safety principles (read before acting)
1) **Traffic shift first, then drain.** Do not drain capacity that is still receiving significant new traffic.
2) **Prefer drain over evac.** Evacuation is higher risk; use only when the region is actively impairing service or the pool is unstable.
3) **Do not flap.** Respect automation hold-down timers and rate limits. Multiple flip/drain cycles worsen customer impact.
4) **Dedicated requires explicit tenant guardrails.** Dedicated pools should not be drained without verifying:
   - Target region capacity reservation/headroom
   - Data residency / contractual constraints
   - Customer comms requirements (if any)
5) **Always keep at least one healthy route.** Ensure routing fallback exists before reducing serving capacity.

---

## Prerequisites / access
You must have:
- Access to internal tooling (CLI + dashboards)
- Ability to read routing policy state and region health
- Permission to initiate pool drain (role: infra-oncall or delegated)

**Tools referenced in this runbook:**
- `failoverctl` (failover controller/operator CLI)
- `poolctl` (fleet pool management CLI)
- Observability dashboards (failover signals, pool saturation, drain progress)

If you do not have access, page **Infra On-Call** and **SRE On-Call**.

---

## Inputs to collect (5–10 minutes)
Capture these before changing anything (paste into incident timeline):

### A) Determine event type
- [ ] **Planned** (game day / scheduled test)
- [ ] **Unplanned** (real impairment)

### B) Identify affected surface area
- [ ] Hosted API routes/models affected (e.g., chat, embeddings)
- [ ] Dedicated tenants affected (list tenant IDs + tiers)
- [ ] Region(s): source region to drain, target region(s)

### C) Confirm routing state (must-have)
From routing team or `failoverctl`:
- Current policy state: is the region already de-preferred / disabled?
- Controller mode: dry-run vs execute; approval required?
- Any hold-down timers active?

### D) Confirm region health signals (corroboration)
- Reachability probes (authoritative)
- 5xx burn + tail latency burn
- Capacity headroom in target region(s)
- Network status / provider status page notes

---

## Decision matrix: Drain vs Evacuate
**Default:** Drain.

Proceed with **Drain** if:
- Routing has shifted or is shifting traffic away
- Region is degraded but not fully unreachable
- Control plane is stable enough to manage pool state

Proceed with **Evacuation** if **any** of the following:
- Region becomes unreachable or intermittently unreachable
- Control plane is failing (cannot reliably schedule/monitor)
- Pool health is collapsing (crash loops, node loss, scheduler failures)
- Continuing to wait for natural drain is increasing customer impact

If unsure, choose **Drain** and re-evaluate after 10 minutes.

---

## Procedure 1: Coordinated drain (recommended)
### Step 1 — Establish coordination + announce intent
- [ ] Confirm incident channel and owner(s): SRE IC + Infra lead
- [ ] Post in incident channel:
  - Region + pool names
  - Drain intent
  - Target region(s)
  - Expected customer impact (ideally none beyond transient retries)

### Step 2 — Ensure routing is shifting away (gate)
**Gate: do not drain until routing is in motion.**

Verify one of:
- Failover controller has executed policy flip away from the region, OR
- Routing on-call confirms manual policy update completed, OR
- For a controlled test: the scheduled routing step is complete

Suggested checks:
- `failoverctl status --region us-east` (example)
- Dashboard: Failover Signals → Policy flips + traffic distribution

Expected state before draining:
- Traffic share in source region trending down
- Target region request rate increasing but within safe headroom

### Step 3 — Verify target region headroom (gate)
**Gate: ensure target can absorb traffic without overload.**

Check:
- GPU utilization and queue depth
- Token latency (p95/p99) and 5xx in target region
- Admission control / circuit breaker status

If target region is near saturation:
- Coordinate with routing to split traffic across multiple regions
- Enable load shedding / stricter retries before draining further

### Step 4 — Initiate drain on the pool
Use pool tooling to stop new placements while allowing in-flight work to complete.

Example:
- `poolctl drain start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "regional_failover" --ttl 60m`

Recommended drain settings:
- **Placement disabled:** on
- **Grace period:** 15–30 minutes for Hosted API pools; 30–60 minutes for Dedicated pools (unless evac is required)
- **TTL:** set to prevent “forgotten drain” (default 60 minutes)

For Dedicated pools, prefer per-tenant drain:
- `poolctl drain start --pool <DEDICATED_POOL_ID> --tenant <TENANT_ID> --ttl 60m`

### Step 5 — Monitor drain progress
Watch until drain completes or stabilizes.

Monitor:
- Active sessions / in-flight requests
- KV cache eviction progress (if available)
- Node health and autoscaler behavior
- Drain progress metric (Dedicated): `dedicated_drain_progress{pool=...}`

Suggested cadence:
- 2–3 minute updates in incident channel

### Step 6 — Validate outcomes
Drain is “successful” when:
- New placements are near zero in the drained pool
- In-flight work trends toward zero without sharp 5xx spikes
- Target region latency/5xx stays within acceptable bounds

If drain causes elevated errors:
- Check gateway retry budgets and circuit breaker status
- Confirm client redirect handling (streaming reconnect)
- Slow down the drain (increase grace / pause) before proceeding

### Step 7 — Lock state and handoff
Once drained:
- Mark pool as drained with a clear tag/annotation
- Ensure routing policy remains stable (respect hold-down)
- Decide whether to keep drained (standby) or proceed to evacuation/scale-down

---

## Procedure 2: Evacuation (higher risk; use when required)
### Step 1 — Confirm evacuation authorization
Evacuation should be approved by:
- SRE IC (or SRE on-call) AND
- Infra on-call lead

If Dedicated customers are impacted, loop in Support liaison (Dev Patel / Owen Phillips) for comms coordination.

### Step 2 — Freeze routing changes (avoid oscillation)
Before aggressive actions, confirm:
- Routing policy is stable and will not automatically revert during evacuation.
- Automation rate limits/anti-flap timers are understood.

If rollback is likely, pause and coordinate with routing.

### Step 3 — Force stop placements and accelerate shutdown
Example:
- `poolctl evacuate start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "region_unreachable" --max-parallel 20 --force-after 10m`

Guidance:
- Limit parallelism to avoid mass reconnect storms.
- For multi-tenant Hosted API pools, prioritize stability over speed.

### Step 4 — Protect target region from overload
During evacuation, expect:
- Retry spikes
- Connection churn
- Increased cold starts and cache misses

Mitigations (coordinate with gateway/routing owners):
- Enforce `Retry-After` overload responses
- Temporarily tighten gateway retry budgets
- Increase admission control strictness to maintain tail latency SLOs

### Step 5 — Validate and complete evacuation
Success criteria:
- Pool has no schedulable capacity
- All nodes are cordoned/removed or otherwise inactive
- Traffic is steady in target region(s)

If control plane is failing and you cannot complete evacuation cleanly:
- Escalate to Control Plane on-call
- Capture evidence and stop making repeated changes

---

## Rollback / abort criteria
Stop and reassess if any of the following occurs:
- Target region enters sustained overload (rapid 5xx increase, severe tail latency burn)
- Routing policy begins oscillating (auto rollback triggers) during drain/evac
- Drain tool reports inconsistent state (stuck drain, missing signals)
- Dedicated tenant violates residency/region constraints (security/compliance risk)

Rollback options (coordinate with routing):
1) Pause drain/evac:
   - `poolctl drain pause --pool <POOL_ID>`
2) Re-enable placements temporarily (only if routing is still sending traffic):
   - `poolctl drain stop --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "rollback"`
3) Slow traffic shift (policy engine changes) rather than reverting fully

Always record who approved rollback and why.

---

## Communication checklist
### Internal
- [ ] Incident channel updates every 5–10 minutes during active drain/evac
- [ ] Incident-bot timeline annotations (verify failover/drain markers are present)
- [ ] Link dashboards used for decisions

### Customer-facing (when applicable)
Hosted API:
- Status page updates are handled by SRE IC per comms playbook.

Dedicated:
- If draining a Dedicated pool that can impact throughput/latency, coordinate with Support/CS for proactive notice per account requirements.

Reference: Regional Failover Communication Playbook.

---

## Post-action validation (required)
After drain/evac is complete:
- [ ] Confirm policy state + traffic distribution is stable for at least 30 minutes
- [ ] Confirm no sustained error budget burn in target region
- [ ] Confirm Dedicated drain progress metrics are clean and saved
- [ ] Ensure pools are either:
  - left drained intentionally with TTL + owner, OR
  - returned to service with an explicit plan

Create follow-up tasks if:
- Drain took longer than expected
- Any transient customer impact occurred (even if within SLO)
- Any manual steps were unclear or tools were missing

---

## Notes on Dedicated vs Hosted
### Dedicated pools
- Drain per tenant/pool; do not batch multiple tenants without explicit approval.
- Verify contract constraints (region pinning) before shifting.
- Prefer “warm standby” capacity in target region if available.

### Hosted API pools
- High concurrency + streaming means connection churn is a primary risk.
- Expect higher cache miss rates after traffic shift; watch tail latency.

---

## Metrics / dashboards to use
During drain/evac, monitor:
- Region traffic split by route/model
- 5xx burn rate and tail latency burn (source + target)
- Reachability probe status (authoritative)
- GPU utilization, queue depth, and admission control rejections
- Drain progress metrics for Dedicated

Dashboards:
- Failover Signals Dashboard (reachability, burn rates, policy flips)
- Fleet Capacity Dashboard (headroom per region/pool)
- Dedicated Drain Progress Dashboard (per tenant/pool)

---

## Appendix A — Example incident timeline snippet
Copy/paste template:
- T+00: Confirmed reachability failures in us-east (probe fail 80%); 5xx burn corroborated.
- T+03: Routing policy flipped us-east weight 100%→0% (failoverctl execution id: …).
- T+06: Verified eu-west headroom (GPU util 62%, queue stable).
- T+08: Initiated pool drain on us-east pool rw-hosted-ue1-a (ttl 60m).
- T+18: Drain progress 70%; no sustained 5xx spikes; target p99 stable.
- T+26: Drain complete; placements disabled; in-flight near zero.

---

## Appendix B — Common failure modes and fixes
1) **Drain appears stuck**
   - Cause: long-lived streaming sessions or stuck workers
   - Action: extend grace period; for evac, set conservative force-after; coordinate with gateway to reduce retries

2) **Target region overload after drain start**
   - Cause: traffic shift too fast + cache miss + retry storm
   - Action: pause drain; split traffic across multiple regions; enable stricter admission control; tune retries

3) **Oscillation (routing flips back and forth)**
   - Cause: noisy signals, hold-down mis-tuned
   - Action: stop making capacity changes; coordinate with routing to stabilize; follow ADR-043 rollback guardrails

4) **Dedicated tenant capacity shortfall**
   - Cause: reservations/headroom insufficient in target region
   - Action: halt drain; allocate burst capacity if available; coordinate with Dedicated product + Support for comms

---

## Change log
- 2026-02-12: Added evacuation guardrails, Dedicated per-tenant guidance, and explicit routing gates; aligned terminology with failover controller audit events.
- 2026-01-20: Initial publication for Q1 game day support.

Content: ## Purpose
This runbook describes how to safely **drain** and, if needed, **evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:
- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)
- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated
- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)

Title: GPU Pool Drain and Evacuation Procedure (Regional Failover / Impairment)
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: eng-infra

evacuate** GPU pools in a region during:
- Regional impairment (cloud/provider incident, network reachability issues, control plane instability)
- Planned or unplanned **regional failover** for Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated
- Capacity protection events (preventing cascading overload when a region becomes unhealthy)

**Drain** means: stop placing new work on a pool and let in-flight work complete (or age out) while routing shifts traffic elsewhere.

**Evacuation** means: drain + expedite termination/migration of remaining workloads (with stricter safeguards), typically when the region is actively failing.

This procedure must be coordinated with routing (policy engine + failover controller) to avoid creating a thundering herd, retry storms, or overload in the target region.

---

## Scope / ownership
**Applies to:**
- Hosted API serving GPU pools (multi-tenant)
- Dedicated customer pools (tenant-isolated)

**Not covered:**
- Customer-managed on-prem clusters (see Private deployment guidance)

**Primary on-call:** Infra (Fleet/Capacity) + SRE

**Key coordination roles:**
- SRE on-call (incident commander / traffic shift approvals)
- Routing/control plane on-call (policy flips, hold-down/rollback)
- Network on-call (reachability validation)
- Dedicated support liaison (customer notifications when required)

---

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when **any** of the following is true:
1) Failover controller recommends or executes regional failover and indicates **pool drain required**.
2) Region health is **UNHEALTHY** (reachability authoritative) and continuing to accept new requests will increase customer impact.
3) GPU pool shows sustained symptoms consistent with regional impairment:
   - Elevated 5xx burn rate + corroborated reachability failures
   - Severe tail latency burn with network symptoms
   - Control plane errors impacting scheduling/placement
4) Planned controlled failover test (game day) includes pool drain/evacuation steps.

## Safety principles (read before acting)
1) **Traffic shift first, then drain.** Do not drain capacity that is still receiving significant new traffic.
2) **Prefer drain over evac.** Evacuation is higher risk; use only when the region is actively impairing service or the pool is unstable.
3) **Do not flap.** Respect automation hold-down timers and rate limits. Multiple flip/drain cycles worsen customer impact.
4) **Dedicated requires explicit tenant guardrails.** Dedicated pools should not be drained without verifying:
   - Target region capacity reservation/headroom
   - Data residency / contractual constraints
   - Customer comms requirements (if any)
5) **Always keep at least one healthy route.** Ensure routing fallback exists before reducing serving capacity.

---

## Prerequisites / access
You must have:
- Access to internal tooling (CLI + dashboards)
- Ability to read routing policy state and region health
- Permission to initiate pool drain (role: infra-oncall or delegated)

**Tools referenced in this runbook:**
- `failoverctl` (failover controller/operator CLI)
- `poolctl` (fleet pool management CLI)
- Observability dashboards (failover signals, pool saturation, drain progress)

If you do not have access, page **Infra On-Call** and **SRE On-Call**.

---

## Decision matrix: Drain vs Evacuate
**Default:** Drain.

Proceed with **Drain** if:
- Routing has shifted or is shifting traffic away
- Region is degraded but not fully unreachable
- Control plane is stable enough to manage pool state

Proceed with **Evacuation** if **any** of the following:
- Region becomes unreachable or intermittently unreachable
- Control plane is failing (cannot reliably schedule/monitor)
- Pool health is collapsing (crash loops, node loss, scheduler failures)
- Continuing to wait for natural drain is increasing customer impact

If unsure, choose **Drain** and re-evaluate after 10 minutes.

---

## Procedure 1: Coordinated drain (recommended)
### Step 1 — Establish coordination + announce intent
- [ ] Confirm incident channel and owner(s): SRE IC + Infra lead
- [ ] Post in incident channel:
  - Region + pool names
  - Drain intent
  - Target region(s)
  - Expected customer impact (ideally none beyond transient retries)

### Step 2 — Ensure routing is shifting away (gate)
**Gate: do not drain until routing is in motion.**

Verify one of:
- Failover controller has executed policy flip away from the region, OR
- Routing on-call confirms manual policy update completed, OR
- For a controlled test: the scheduled routing step is complete

Suggested checks:
- `failoverctl status --region us-east` (example)
- Dashboard: Failover Signals → Policy flips + traffic distribution

Expected state before draining:
- Traffic share in source region trending down
- Target region request rate increasing but within safe headroom

### Step 3 — Verify target region headroom (gate)
**Gate: ensure target can absorb traffic without overload.**

Check:
- GPU utilization and queue depth
- Token latency (p95/p99) and 5xx in target region
- Admission control / circuit breaker status

If target region is near saturation:
- Coordinate with routing to split traffic across multiple regions
- Enable load shedding / stricter retries before draining further

### Step 4 — Initiate drain on the pool
Use pool tooling to stop new placements while allowing in-flight work to complete.

Example:
- `poolctl drain start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "regional_failover" --ttl 60m`

Recommended drain settings:
- **Placement disabled:** on
- **Grace period:** 15–30 minutes for Hosted API pools; 30–60 minutes for Dedicated pools (unless evac is required)
- **TTL:** set to prevent “forgotten drain” (default 60 minutes)

For Dedicated pools, prefer per-tenant drain:
- `poolctl drain start --pool <DEDICATED_POOL_ID> --tenant <TENANT_ID> --ttl 60m`

### Step 6 — Validate outcomes
Drain is “successful” when:
- New placements are near zero in the drained pool
- In-flight work trends toward zero without sharp 5xx spikes
- Target region latency/5xx stays within acceptable bounds

If drain causes elevated errors:
- Check gateway retry budgets and circuit breaker status
- Confirm client redirect handling (streaming reconnect)
- Slow down the drain (increase grace / pause) before proceeding

### Step 7 — Lock state and handoff
Once drained:
- Mark pool as drained with a clear tag/annotation
- Ensure routing policy remains stable (respect hold-down)
- Decide whether to keep drained (standby) or proceed to evacuation/scale-down

---

## Procedure 2: Evacuation (higher risk; use when required)
### Step 1 — Confirm evacuation authorization
Evacuation should be approved by:
- SRE IC (or SRE on-call) AND
- Infra on-call lead

If Dedicated customers are impacted, loop in Support liaison (Dev Patel / Owen Phillips) for comms coordination.

### Step 2 — Freeze routing changes (avoid oscillation)
Before aggressive actions, confirm:
- Routing policy is stable and will not automatically revert during evacuation.
- Automation rate limits/anti-flap timers are understood.

If rollback is likely, pause and coordinate with routing.

### Step 2 — Freeze routing changes (avoid oscillation)
Before aggressive actions, confirm:
- Routing policy is stable and will not automatically revert during evacuation.
- Automation rate limits/anti-flap timers are understood.

If rollback is likely, pause and coordinate with routing.

### Step 3 — Force stop placements and accelerate shutdown
Example:
- `poolctl evacuate start --pool <POOL_ID> --reason "region_unreachable" --max-parallel 20 --force-after 10m`

Guidance:
- Limit parallelism to avoid mass reconnect storms.
- For multi-tenant Hosted API pools, prioritize stability over speed.

### Step 4 — Protect target region from overload
During evacuation, expect:
- Retry spikes
- Connection churn
- Increased cold starts and cache misses

Mitigations (coordinate with gateway/routing owners):
- Enforce `Retry-After` overload responses
- Temporarily tighten gateway retry budgets
- Increase admission control strictness to maintain tail latency SLOs

### Step 5 — Validate and complete evacuation
Success criteria:
- Pool has no schedulable capacity
- All nodes are cordoned/removed or otherwise inactive
- Traffic is steady in target region(s)

If control plane is failing and you cannot complete evacuation cleanly:
- Escalate to Control Plane on-call
- Capture evidence and stop making repeated changes

---

## Rollback / abort criteria
Stop and reassess if any of the following occurs:
- Target region enters sustained overload (rapid 5xx increase, severe tail latency burn)
- Routing policy begins oscillating (auto rollback triggers) during drain/evac
- Drain tool reports inconsistent state (stuck drain, missing signals)
- Dedicated tenant violates residency/region constraints (security/compliance risk)

1) Pause drain/evac:

3) Slow traffic shift (policy engine changes) rather than reverting fully

Always record who approved rollback and why.

- [ ] Incident channel updates every 5–10 minutes during active drain/evac
- [ ] Incident-bot timeline annotations (verify failover/drain markers are present)

- Status page updates are handled by SRE IC per comms playbook.

Dedicated:
- If draining a Dedicated pool that can impact throughput/latency, coordinate with Support/CS for proactive notice per account requirements.

Reference: Regional Failover Communication Playbook.

After drain/evac is complete:
- [ ] Confirm policy state + traffic distribution is stable for at least 30 minutes
- [ ] Confirm no sustained error budget burn in target region
- [ ] Confirm Dedicated drain progress metrics are clean and saved
- [ ] Ensure pools are either:
  - left drained intentionally with TTL + owner, OR
  - returned to service with an explicit plan

Create follow-up tasks if:

- Any transient customer impact occurred (even if within SLO)

## Notes on Dedicated vs Hosted
### Dedicated pools
- Drain per tenant/pool; do not batch multiple tenants without explicit approval.
- Verify contract constraints (region pinning) before shifting.
- Prefer “warm standby” capacity in target region if available.

### Hosted API pools
- High concurrency + streaming means connection churn is a primary risk.
- Expect higher cache miss rates after traffic shift; watch tail latency.

---

## Metrics / dashboards to use
During drain/evac, monitor:
- Region traffic split by route/model
- 5xx burn rate and tail latency burn (source + target)
- Reachability probe status (authoritative)
- GPU utilization, queue depth, and admission control rejections
- Drain progress metrics for Dedicated

Dashboards:
- Failover Signals Dashboard (reachability, burn rates, policy flips)
- Fleet Capacity Dashboard (headroom per region/pool)
- Dedicated Drain Progress Dashboard (per tenant/pool)

---

## Appendix B — Common failure modes and fixes
1) **Drain appears stuck**
   - Cause: long-lived streaming sessions or stuck workers
   - Action: extend grace period; for evac, set conservative force-after; coordinate with gateway to reduce retries

2) **Target region overload after drain start**
   - Cause: traffic shift too fast + cache miss + retry storm
   - Action: pause drain; split traffic across multiple regions; enable stricter admission control; tune retries

3) **Oscillation (routing flips back and forth)**
   - Cause: noisy signals, hold-down mis-tuned
   - Action: stop making capacity changes; coordinate with routing to stabilize; follow ADR-043 rollback guardrails

4) **Dedicated tenant capacity shortfall**
   - Cause: reservations/headroom insufficient in target region
   - Action: halt drain; allocate burst capacity if available; coordinate with Dedicated product + Support for comms
